components.detail: Mostly pale two-row, kept simple so the hops dominate.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Massive Simcoe, Citra, Columbus, and Mosaic charges across boil and dry hop.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Highly attenuative American ale yeast to avoid a syrupy finish.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Dextrose or corn sugar boosts strength without adding body.

composition.process: Multiple large late-hop and dry-hop additions layered over a fast, dry fermentation.

name: English IPA
description: The ancestral form of all IPAs, earthier and more restrained than its American descendants. Its lineage traces to pale ales that survived the long sea voyage to India.
origin: London and Burton upon Trent, England
funFact: George Hodgson's Bow Brewery in London dominated the late-1700s beer trade to India, laying the groundwork for the style's legend.

serve.how: Serve it English-style: cool, not cold, in a nonic pint with a modest, creamy head from a gentle pour. The earthy hops, marmalade, and biscuit notes only show themselves above fridge temperature, so give a cold bottle 20 minutes on the counter. Sip steadily and notice the tea-like hop finish — restraint and balance are the style's virtues, not punch.

composition.summary: Maris Otter pale malt hopped hard with earthy English varieties and English ale yeast.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Maris Otter or Golden Promise with a light crystal touch.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: East Kent Goldings, Fuggle, and Target — earthy, marmalade, tea-like.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: English ale yeast leaving fruity esters and a rounder mouthfeel.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Sulfate-heavy Burton water sharpens the bitterness into a dry snap.

composition.process: Warm fermentation with heavy kettle hopping and traditional dry hopping in cask or tank.

name: Milkshake IPA
description: A dessert-adjacent mutation thickened with lactose and often fruit or vanilla. Divides trainers into devoted collectors and horrified traditionalists.
funFact: The style emerged from a 2015 collaboration between Pennsylvania's Tired Hands Brewing and Sweden's Omnipollo.

serve.how: Gently roll the can before opening to rouse any settled fruit and lactose, then pour slowly into a tulip to showcase the opaque, creamy body. Serve it slightly warmer than a standard IPA so the vanilla and tropical fruit bloom instead of hiding behind the chill. Treat it like dessert in a glass — one is usually the right number, sipped slowly.

composition.summary: A hazy IPA thickened with lactose and loaded with fruit purée and vanilla.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale malt with oats and wheat for a soft, opaque body.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Citra, Galaxy, and Mosaic added late for tropical aroma.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Fruity English-derived hazy strains that stay soft and low-attenuating.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Lactose for body and sweetness, plus fruit purée and vanilla.

composition.process: Fruit and lactose go in after fermentation so the sweetness survives to the can.

name: New England IPA
description: A hazy, juice-bomb variant that traded bitterness for pillowy softness and orange-juice opacity. Emerged from Vermont and rapidly displaced its clearer cousins.
funFact: The Alchemist's Heady Topper is widely credited as the style's prototype, and the Brewers Association added 'Juicy or Hazy IPA' as an official category in 2018.

serve.how: Pour slowly and steadily into a tulip and admire the orange-juice opacity — a NEIPA should look like a glass of hazy sunrise. Drink it as close to the canning date as you can find; the mango and stone-fruit aromatics fade within weeks. Skip big swirls and just take soft, pillowy sips, noticing how the bitterness stays gentle while the juice does the talking.

composition.summary: Oat- and wheat-softened pale malt saturated with late-addition and dry hops.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Two-row pale with heavy flaked oats and wheat for a pillowy body.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Citra, Mosaic, Galaxy, Nelson — whirlpool and double dry hop, minimal bittering.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: London or Vermont strains that stay in suspension and throw stone fruit.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Chloride dialed above sulfate in the water for a rounder mouthfeel.

composition.process: Dry hopping during active fermentation drives biotransformation into that juice-like aroma.

name: Session IPA
description: A lightweight forme of the IPA bred for endurance rather than power. Delivers full hop aroma at an ABV that permits repeat encounters.
funFact: Founders All Day IPA popularized the style and its 15-pack became one of the best-selling craft beer packages in America.

serve.how: Serve it well chilled in a pint glass with an easy pour and a finger of foam — this is a beer engineered for the long haul, not ceremony. The citrus-zest aroma is the payoff, so drink it fresh and don't let it sit and warm. Its light cracker body and low ABV make it the right call for an afternoon of yard work, cards, or a second and third round.

composition.summary: A low-gravity pale malt base carrying a full-size American hop load.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Light two-row or pilsner malt with a little wheat for body.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Cascade, Citra, and Amarillo at full IPA aroma rates, moderate bitterness.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean, attenuative American ale yeast.

composition.process: Brewed to low gravity, then dry hopped as heavily as a full-strength IPA.

name: Triple IPA
description: The final evolution of the hop-forward line, a syrupy titan north of ten percent. Encountered mostly at special releases, where it draws crowds of trainers.
funFact: Russian River's Pliny the Younger, released for just two weeks each February, has drawn multi-hour lines and beer tourists from around the world.

serve.how: Pour a modest measure into a snifter and cup the bowl in your palm — a little warmth unlocks the honeyed malt beneath the dank resin. Swirl gently and nose it like a spirit before each sip; at 10-13% this is a slow, contemplative pour, not a pint. Split a bottle with a friend and notice how the candied grapefruit fights the warming alcohol all the way down.

composition.summary: A hop-saturated ale of enormous gravity, thinned with sugar to stay drinkable.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale two-row in huge quantity with almost no specialty malt.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Pounds per barrel of Simcoe, Citra, Columbus, and Nelson at every stage.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: High-alcohol-tolerant American ale yeast, usually stepped up first.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Corn sugar or dextrose dries out a wort this big.

composition.process: Multiple dry-hop rounds over a high-gravity fermentation pushed to full attenuation.

name: West Coast IPA
description: A crystal-clear, bone-dry evolution of the IPA that attacks with pine and grapefruit. Prized by purists for its aggressive bitterness and total lack of haze.
funFact: Russian River brewer Vinnie Cilurzo coined the term 'lupulin threshold shift' to describe hopheads' ever-growing tolerance for bitterness.

serve.how: Pour assertively into a spotless pint glass and hold it up first — brilliant clarity is this style's badge of honor. Serve it chilled but not frigid so the pine and grapefruit pith cut through with maximum aroma, and drink it fresh while the hops are loud. Chase the long, dry, bitter finish; a proper West Coast should scrub the palate clean and demand the next sip.

composition.summary: Clean pale malt, sulfate-crisp water, and piney American hops at hard bitterness.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Two-row pale with minimal crystal — the malt is scaffolding, not flavor.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Chinook, Simcoe, Centennial, Columbus — pine, grapefruit pith, dank resin.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean, highly attenuative American ale yeast for a bone-dry finish.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Sulfate-forward water accentuates the bitter snap.

composition.process: Aggressive kettle bittering plus dry hopping, then fined or filtered to full clarity.

name: American Pale Ale
description: The friendly ambassador of craft beer, balancing biscuity malt against bright citrus hops. Often the first wild hop-creature a new drinker encounters.
funFact: Sierra Nevada Pale Ale, first brewed in Chico in 1980 with Cascade hops, essentially defined the style for American craft brewing.

serve.how: Pour with confidence into a pint glass to raise a creamy head that lifts the floral, grapefruit hop aroma. Serve it just above fridge-cold — a few minutes on the counter lets the biscuity malt step forward and show the balance the style is famous for. This is the everyday benchmark beer: taste for hops and malt in genuine equilibrium, neither one shouting.

composition.summary: Pale two-row with light crystal, hopped with citrusy American varieties, fermented warm.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Two-row pale with a small crystal addition for biscuit and color.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Cascade above all — grapefruit and pine — plus Centennial or Amarillo.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean American ale yeast, low in esters.

composition.process: Warm ale fermentation with late kettle and dry hop additions for aroma.

name: Blonde Ale
description: A gentle, sun-colored species that hides in plain sight on nearly every taproom menu. Low bitterness and a soft malt sweetness make it approachable to all trainers.
funFact: Brewers affectionately call blonde ale a 'lawnmower beer'—a gateway style designed to lure lager drinkers into the craft world.

serve.how: Serve it cold in a pint glass with an easy, medium-fast pour and a thin white cap — no ritual required, which is exactly its charm. Look for gentle honey and fresh bread on the nose and a soft, clean swallow with barely-there bitterness. It is the ideal porch and lawnmower beer: unfussy, refreshing, and welcoming to whoever you hand one to.

composition.summary: A simple pale malt grist, lightly hopped, fermented clean with ale yeast.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Two-row or pilsner malt, sometimes a little wheat or honey malt.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Willamette, Cascade, or noble hops at gentle bitterness.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean American ale yeast fermented cool for minimal esters.

composition.process: A straightforward warm fermentation, often cold conditioned for lager-like clarity.

name: English Pale Ale
description: The dignified elder of the pale ale line, favoring toffee malt and earthy hops over flash. Evolves best at cellar temperature, where its fruity esters emerge.
funFact: Brewers worldwide still add gypsum to their water to mimic Burton's mineral-rich wells, a process known as 'Burtonisation.'

serve.how: Pour gently into a nonic pint at cellar temperature — served too cold, the toffee and marmalade character simply refuses to show up. Aim for a low, creamy head and take relaxed, pub-paced swallows rather than analytical sips. As it warms further, watch the fruity esters and mineral, Burton-water snap emerge; this beer improves across the whole glass.

composition.summary: Maris Otter and crystal malt with earthy English hops and expressive ale yeast.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Maris Otter pale malt with crystal for toffee depth.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: East Kent Goldings and Fuggle — earthy, floral, marmalade.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: English ale yeast leaving pear and orange esters.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Burtonised, sulfate-rich water gives the classic mineral dryness.

composition.process: Warm fermentation and conditioning at cellar temperature, traditionally on cask.

name: American Ice Lager
description: A mass-market lager chilled below freezing so ice crystals form and are removed, nudging the strength up. A gas-station descendant of the noble eisbock.
funFact: Labatt launched the first mass-market ice beer in 1993, setting off the short but fierce 'Ice Beer Wars' among North American mega-breweries.

serve.glass: Pint glass or straight from the can
serve.how: Serve it as cold as your fridge will go — near-freezing service is true to both its name and its virtues. Pour it briskly into a cold pint glass if you're feeling formal, but the can is a perfectly authentic vessel. Expect smooth, sweet grain with a faint alcohol warmth; this is a beer for drinking, not dissecting, so pair it with a game and good company.

composition.summary: A standard American adjunct lager frozen and partially de-iced to raise its strength.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Six-row or two-row base malt at a modest rate.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Minimal — bitterness kept low enough to go unnoticed.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Industrial lager yeast fermented cold and fast.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Corn or rice adjuncts keep the flavor light and the cost lower.

composition.process: Chilled below freezing so ice crystals form and are filtered out, concentrating alcohol.

name: American Lager
description: The most-encountered beer creature in North America, found in every stadium, cooler, and dive. Light, fizzy, and inoffensive by careful design.
funFact: Corn and rice entered the recipe in the 1800s because protein-heavy American six-row barley made hazy, heavy beer — the adjuncts lightened the body and clarified the glass.

serve.how: Serve it ice cold with a fast center pour into a frosted or well-chilled pint glass, building a short-lived white head and plenty of carbonic sparkle. Drink it promptly — its crisp, light-grain character is best in the first cold minutes and dullest once warm. Don't overthink it: this is the beer of stadiums and coolers, engineered for effortless refreshment.

composition.summary: Base malt cut heavily with corn or rice, barely hopped, fermented cold and filtered.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Six-row barley malt as the enzyme engine, kept very pale.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: A whisper of Cluster, Willamette, or hop extract.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean industrial lager yeast fermented cold.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Corn grits or rice make up a large share of the grist.

composition.process: Cereal mashing of the adjuncts, then cold fermentation and filtration to bright clarity.

name: American Light Lager
description: An American lager put through an even finer sieve — fewer calories, fewer carbs, and flavor dialed down to a whisper. Its natural habitat is the tailgate.
funFact: Biochemist Joseph Owades invented light beer in 1967 as Gablinger's Diet Beer; the recipe flopped, was given away, and eventually became Miller Lite.

serve.glass: Pint glass or straight from the can
serve.how: The colder the better — serve it near-freezing, straight from the bottom of the cooler, in a chilled glass or right from the can. The flavor is intentionally a whisper of corn and clean fizz, so freshness and frigid temperature are everything. This is hydration-adjacent tailgate fuel: crack it, drink it cold, and reach for the next one before this one warms.

composition.summary: An adjunct lager pushed further — enzymes strip sugars for fewer calories and carbs.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: A small charge of pale base malt; the grist is deliberately thin.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Nearly nothing — a few bitterness units for structure.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean lager yeast fermented cold, then filtered hard.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Rice or corn plus enzymes that convert residual sugars into fermentable ones.

composition.process: Enzyme-assisted fermentation drives attenuation close to total, then heavy filtration.

name: Czech Pilsner
description: The golden original that every pale lager on Earth descends from. Soft Bohemian water and Saaz hops give it a rounded, almost buttery bitterness that has been imitated for nearly two centuries.
funFact: The first batch was brewed in 1842 by Josef Groll, a Bavarian brewer hired by the citizens of Plzeň — making the world's first golden lager a German-Czech collaboration.

serve.how: Pour Czech-style: tilt the glass, then straighten it mid-pour to crown the beer with two to three fingers of dense, wet foam — the head is considered part of the drink in Plzeň. Serve chilled but not ice cold so the bready malt and floral Saaz hops stay expressive. Sip through the foam and notice the rounded, almost buttery soft bitterness that every pale lager on Earth has tried to copy.

composition.summary: Bohemian pilsner malt and Saaz hops, decoction mashed and lagered in soft water.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Floor-malted Bohemian pilsner malt — bready and faintly sweet.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Saaz in all three additions: spicy, floral, rounded bitterness.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Czech lager yeast fermented cold, usually with a diacetyl rest.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Plzeň's exceptionally soft water keeps the bitterness smooth, never sharp.

composition.process: Triple decoction mashing followed by weeks of cold lagering in horizontal tanks.

name: Dortmunder Export
description: The lager that powered Germany's industrial heartland — slightly stronger and rounder than a pils, slightly drier than a helles. A beer engineered for people who worked hard and drank accordingly.
funFact: At its mid-20th-century peak, Dortmund brewed more beer than any other city in Germany, most of it drunk by the coal and steel workers of the Ruhr.

serve.how: Pour steadily into a pokal to build a firm white head atop the deep-gold beer, then let it rest a moment before the first swallow. Serve it chilled but give it room to warm slightly — the biscuit malt and mineral snap are subtle and easily numbed by cold. Drink it in honest working-class measures and appreciate the engineering: rounder than a pils, drier than a helles, balanced to keep going.

composition.summary: Pilsner malt in hard, mineral water with noble hops balanced between pils and helles.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: German pilsner malt, sometimes a small Munich portion for body.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Hallertau or Tettnang at moderate bitterness — balanced, not sharp.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean German lager yeast fermented cold.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Dortmund's hard, sulfate- and carbonate-rich water gives the mineral backbone.

composition.process: Cold fermentation and long lagering to a firm, dry, mineral finish.

name: Festbier
description: The golden, deceptively strong lager actually served at modern Oktoberfest. It drinks like a helles that has been quietly working out.
funFact: This paler style displaced the darker märzen as the official Oktoberfest pour in the 1990s, and only six Munich breweries are permitted to serve beer at the festival.

serve.how: Pour generously into a masskrug or hefty mug with a thick cap of foam — this beer is made for celebratory volume, so don't be shy. Serve it chilled and note the lightly toasty golden malt that drinks smooth and clean while quietly hiding six percent strength. Toast properly, clink at the base of the mug, and pace yourself; the deceptive drinkability is the famous trap.

composition.summary: Pilsner and Munich malt with noble hops, lagered cold for months before the tents open.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: German pilsner base with Munich and Vienna for golden depth.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Hallertau Mittelfrüh at modest levels; balance is the whole point.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Bavarian lager yeast fermented cool and clean.

composition.process: Brewed in spring and lagered for months so a strong beer drinks effortlessly.

name: German Pilsner
description: The Czech original's leaner, drier northern cousin. Crisper water and a sharper hop snap make it finish like a knife — clean, bitter, and gone.
funFact: Pils is by far Germany's best-selling beer style, accounting for roughly half of all beer sold in the country.

serve.how: Pour hard down the center of a tall, narrow pilsner glass to raise a dense two-finger cap of white foam, then let it settle before topping up. The head is part of the drink — sip through it and notice the cracker-dry malt giving way to a sharp herbal hop bite. Serve it fresh and cold; this style is all about the clean, bitter snap of the finish, so don't let it warm past cool.

composition.summary: German pilsner malt with high noble hopping, fermented cold in low-carbonate water.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: German pilsner malt alone — cracker-dry, no specialty malts.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Hallertau, Tettnang, Spalt, or Perle: firm bitterness, herbal aroma.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean German lager yeast fermented cold.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Soft, low-carbonate water lets the bitterness finish clean rather than harsh.

composition.process: Long cold lagering to a crisp, sharply attenuated dry finish.

name: India Pale Lager
description: What happens when an IPA's hop bill is grafted onto a lager's clean, cold skeleton. All the aroma, none of the fruity yeast noise.
funFact: The IPL emerged from American craft brewing around the early 2010s, and brewers still argue over whether it is a true style or just a very good idea.

serve.how: Pour with a moderate tilt into a pint glass, finishing upright to build about an inch of head that pushes the citrus and pine aromatics up to your nose. Drink it fresher than almost anything else in your fridge — hop aroma fades by the week. Notice how the bitterness reads cleaner and snappier than an IPA's because the cold lager fermentation strips away the fruity yeast character.

composition.summary: An IPA-scale hop bill built on a clean pilsner malt base with lager yeast.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pilsner or two-row pale malt, kept simple and dry.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: American or New Zealand varieties in whirlpool and dry hop at IPA rates.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Lager yeast fermented cold, contributing no fruit of its own.

composition.process: Cold lager fermentation, then dry hopping and lagering to drop it bright.

name: Italian Pilsner
description: A German pils that studied abroad and came back better dressed. Dry-hopping with noble German hops adds a floral perfume no traditional pils would dare.
funFact: The style traces to a single beer: Tipopils, first brewed in 1996 by Agostino Arioli at Birrificio Italiano near Como.

serve.how: Pour down the middle of a pilsner glass for a tall, tight head, then bring it straight to your nose — the dry-hopped floral perfume is the whole point of the style. Sip slowly and pick out white pepper and lemongrass over the crisp, dry base. Let it warm just a few degrees from fridge-cold and the noble-hop aromatics bloom noticeably.

composition.summary: German pilsner malt and noble hops, lagered cold and then dry hopped.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: German or Italian pilsner malt — lean and cracker-dry.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Hallertau, Spalt, or Saphir used for both bittering and dry hop.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean German lager yeast fermented cold.

composition.process: Traditional pils brewing plus a noble-hop dry hop — the style's one heresy.

name: Japanese Rice Lager
description: A lager honed to a razor's edge with rice in the grist, prized for a bone-dry finish the Japanese call karakuchi. Its true power is making the next bite of food taste better.
funFact: Asahi Super Dry's 1987 launch triggered Japan's 'Dry Wars,' with every major brewery rushing out its own super-dry lager within a year.

serve.how: Stash the glass in the freezer for ten minutes, then pour briskly down the center for a crisp head — this is one of the few beers that genuinely rewards being ice cold. Take a sip, then a bite of food, then another sip: the bone-dry karakuchi finish is engineered to scrub your palate clean between bites. Notice how the rice keeps the body featherlight and the finish snaps shut with almost no aftertaste.

composition.summary: Pale malt cut with a large rice portion, lightly hopped, fermented very dry.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale barley malt as the base, kept minimal and light.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Low and restrained — often noble or Japanese-grown varieties.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Highly attenuative lager yeast pushed to a bone-dry finish.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Rice in the grist strips body and residual sugar for the karakuchi snap.

composition.process: Cereal-mashed rice plus very high attenuation produce the razor-dry finish.

name: Kellerbier
description: Lager in its natural, unpolished state — unfiltered, gently carbonated, and hazy like it just woke up. Best encountered in a Franconian beer garden under chestnut trees.
funFact: The name means 'cellar beer'; it is traditionally left ungespundet — unbunged — so excess carbonation escapes the barrel, giving it a signature gentle fizz.

serve.how: Pour the whole bottle in one gentle, steady motion into a stoneware mug, haze and all — swirl the last inch to rouse the yeast and add it in. Don't over-chill it; at cellar-cool temperature the fresh-dough and hop-sap character opens up the way it would in a Franconian beer garden. The carbonation is naturally soft, so expect a pillowy texture rather than fizz, and drink it while it's fresh.

composition.summary: An ordinary Franconian lager grist left unfiltered and only lightly carbonated.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Franconian pilsner or Munich malt, depending on pale or amber version.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Fresh German hops at generous rates — Hersbrucker, Spalt, Tettnang.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Bavarian lager yeast left in suspension for a hazy, bready character.

composition.process: Lagered in unbunged casks so excess CO2 escapes, then served unfiltered and soft.

name: Mexican Lager
description: A sun-adapted lager often brewed with flaked maize, born when Central European brewers set up shop in 19th-century Mexico. Frequently spotted wearing a lime wedge.
funFact: Mexico is the world's largest exporter of beer, shipping more abroad than any other country.

serve.how: Serve it thoroughly chilled in a pint glass with a modest head, or keep it in the ice-cold bottle if that's the vibe. A wedge of lime squeezed in and dropped through the neck is traditional and genuinely works — the acid brightens the light corn sweetness. This is a sunshine beer: don't overthink it, just notice the crisp, faintly sweet maize note and how effortlessly it disappears.

composition.summary: Pilsner or Vienna malt lightened with flaked maize, lightly hopped and lagered cold.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pilsner malt for pale versions; Vienna and Munich for the darker ones.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Low bittering from Saaz, Hallertau, or Cluster.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean lager yeast fermented cold.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Flaked maize or corn syrup thins the body for hot-weather drinking.

composition.process: Cold fermentation and lagering, with cereal-mashed corn in traditional versions.

name: Munich Helles
description: Bavaria's gentle everyday lager, built to showcase malt rather than hops. It goes down so easily that a liter feels like a suggestion rather than a commitment.
funFact: Spaten released the first helles in 1894 as Munich's defensive answer to the wildly popular pilsners arriving from Bohemia.

serve.how: Pour with confidence into a heavy mug, building a thick cap of foam you can drink through — in Munich the head is non-negotiable. Serve it cold but a shade warmer than a pilsner so the honeyed, fresh-bread malt has room to show itself. Take long, unhurried draughts rather than analytical sips; this beer is built for easy conversation, and its balance reveals itself over a full glass.

composition.summary: Pilsner and Munich malt with just enough noble hops, lagered cold for weeks.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: German pilsner malt with a Munich touch — soft bread and honey.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Hallertau Mittelfrüh, low: present only to keep it from cloying.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Bavarian lager yeast fermented cold and clean.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Munich's carbonate water historically favored malt over hop bitterness.

composition.process: Step or decoction mashing, then four to eight weeks of cold lagering.

name: Pre-Prohibition Lager
description: A ghost from before 1920: the fuller, hoppier corn lager Americans drank before Prohibition wiped the recipe books clean. Modern brewers resurrect it like brewing archaeology.
funFact: The style was reconstructed largely by homebrewers digging through pre-Prohibition brewing logs, which showed far more hops than any modern American lager uses.

serve.how: Pour into a pint glass with a firm head and give it a moment — this is a fuller, hoppier animal than any modern American lager. Notice the rounded corn-grits sweetness in the middle and the surprisingly assertive grassy hop bite on the finish; that's the historical recipe talking. Let it climb a few degrees as you drink and the malt depth that Prohibition erased comes back into focus.

composition.summary: Six-row barley and corn grits hopped far harder than any modern American lager.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Six-row barley malt, protein-rich and heavy with enzymes.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Cluster and imported noble hops at bitterness modern drinkers find startling.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean American lager yeast fermented cold.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Corn grits, up to a third of the grist, cut the protein haze.

composition.process: Cereal mashing the corn grits, then cold fermentation and long lagering.

name: Zoigl
description: A communal lager brewed in shared village brewhouses of the Upper Palatinate, then fermented and served in private homes on a rotating schedule. Less a beer style than a social institution.
funFact: A six-pointed Zoigl star hung outside a house signals that this week's batch is being poured there — a system still running in a handful of towns like Windischeschenbach and Neuhaus.

serve.how: Treat it like the communal cellar beer it is: pour generously into a stoneware mug, cloudiness included, and don't chase a perfect head — rustic is the point. Serve cellar-cool so the hay, earthy hops, and yeasty bread notes stay open rather than muted. Best drunk with company and food on the table, the way it's poured under the six-pointed star in the Oberpfalz.

composition.summary: A rustic unfiltered Bavarian lager brewed communally and fermented in private home cellars.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Bavarian pilsner and Munich malt, often locally floor-malted.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Regional German hops — Hersbrucker or Spalt — modest and earthy.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: House lager yeast passed between families; hazy and bready.

composition.process: Wort brewed in a shared village brewhouse, then fermented and lagered in each family's own cellar.

name: American Porter
description: A robust revival of London's lost workhorse beer, rebuilt with more roast and American hops. Sits between brown ale and stout on the darkness spectrum.
funFact: Anchor Porter, launched in 1972, helped resurrect the style in America decades after Prohibition had all but wiped it out.

serve.how: Take it out of the fridge fifteen minutes before pouring, then pour steadily into a pint glass for a tan, creamy head. Too cold and it tastes thin and roasty; at cellar-ish temperature the cocoa, coffee, and caramel layers separate and become easy to pick apart. Sip, let it coat your palate, and notice how the American hops keep the roast from turning sweet.

composition.summary: Pale malt with chocolate and black malt, hopped with assertive American varieties.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Two-row pale with chocolate malt, black malt, and crystal for depth.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: American varieties at real bitterness — Chinook, Cascade, Willamette.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean American ale yeast that keeps the roast in focus.

composition.process: Warm ale fermentation with a firmer hop bill than any English porter would carry.

name: Baltic Porter
description: A smooth, powerful porter that evolved around the cold Baltic Sea, where it adopted lager fermentation. Silky dark fruit and licorice with none of the rough edges.
funFact: Despite the name, most Baltic porters are technically lagers—local brewers copied strong English export porters but fermented them cold with lager yeast.

serve.how: Pour gently into a snifter, leaving any sediment behind, and cup the bowl in your hand to nudge it warmer as you go. Swirl and nose it like a dessert wine — the lager fermentation makes it uncannily smooth, so the dark fruit, licorice, and toffee arrive without any burn. This is a slow, contemplative pour; one bottle split between two glasses is the right pace.

composition.summary: A strong dark grist of Munich and roasted malts fermented cold with lager yeast.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Munich and pilsner base with chocolate, black, and caramel malts.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Continental noble hops, used for bittering only.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Lager yeast fermented cold — the reason it's so smooth at strength.

composition.process: Cold lager fermentation and months of lagering strip the harshness from a huge dark beer.

name: English Porter
description: The original dark beer of the industrial age, softer and more chocolatey than its stout descendants. Once the fuel of an entire laboring city.
funFact: The beer takes its name from the street and river porters of 1700s London who adopted it, and it is often called the world's first industrially brewed style.

serve.how: Pour into a nonic pint with a relaxed hand, aiming for a finger of tan foam, and resist the urge to serve it fridge-cold — cellar temperature is where the milk chocolate and toffee live. Drink it in proper pub measures, steady and social, noticing how soft the roast is compared to a stout. The gentle carbonation and modest strength make it a beer for the whole evening.

composition.summary: Pale malt with brown, chocolate, and crystal malts, hopped gently with English varieties.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale malt with brown malt, chocolate malt, and crystal for cocoa softness.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Fuggle and Goldings at low, earthy bitterness.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: English ale yeast leaving light stone-fruit esters.

composition.process: Warm ale fermentation; historically the beer was blended from aged and fresh batches.

name: Smoked Porter
description: A porter infused with the campfire aura of smoked malt. Encountered near barbecue and bonfires, it splits opinion like few other dark types.
funFact: Alaskan Brewing's influential Smoked Porter, first released in 1988, uses malt smoked over local alder wood—the same wood used for Alaskan salmon.

serve.how: Pour into a pint glass and give it a minute before the first sip — smoke aromatics are volatile and shift as the beer warms. Early on you'll get campfire and bacon; as it opens, chocolate and roast rise up underneath. If you're new to smoked beer, drink it alongside grilled or smoked food, which makes the woodsmoke read as seasoning instead of the whole show.

composition.summary: A porter grist carrying a portion of wood-smoked malt alongside the dark malts.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale and chocolate malt plus smoked malt — alder, beech, or cherrywood.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Modest English or American bittering; smoke and roast lead.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean ale yeast so the smoke stays legible.

components.label: Other
components.detail: The wood defines the character: alder is sweeter, beech sharper.

composition.process: Smoked malt is blended at anywhere from ten to a hundred percent of the grist.

name: Scottish Ale
description: A malt-forward creature of the cold north, where hops were expensive imports and sweetness ruled. Sessionable, coppery, and quietly caramelized.
funFact: The traditional names 60/-, 70/-, and 80/- (shilling) come from the 19th-century wholesale price per cask, which rose with the beer's strength.

serve.how: Pour into a nonic pint with a gentle tilt for a modest, creamy head — this is a low-carbonation, malt-first beer that doesn't want a towering cap of foam. Serve at cellar temperature so the caramel and toffee show fully; cold mutes exactly the notes the style is built on. Sip steadily and notice how little bitterness there is, just layers of toasted, lightly sweet malt.

composition.summary: Scottish pale malt with caramel malt and a hint of roasted barley, barely hopped.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Golden Promise or Maris Otter with crystal and a touch of roasted barley.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: East Kent Goldings or Fuggle at very low rates — hops were expensive imports.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Scottish ale yeast fermented cool, keeping esters restrained.

composition.process: A long boil caramelizes the wort, then cool fermentation keeps the profile malt-forward.

name: Wee Heavy
description: The Scottish ale's fully evolved form: a rich, warming malt bomb with notes of caramel and dark fruit. Small in serving size, heavy in every other respect.
funFact: Also called Scotch ale, it is traditionally served in a thistle-shaped glass modeled on Scotland's national flower.

serve.how: Pour slowly into a thistle glass — or a snifter — filling only two-thirds so you can swirl and nose the caramel, plum, and whisper of smoke. Serve it warmer than any other beer in your fridge; straight from cold it hides everything, but near 60°F it turns plush and dessert-like. Small pours, slow sips: it drinks like a nightcap, and the alcohol warmth on the finish is part of the experience.

composition.summary: A huge Scottish malt bill boiled long and fermented cool for caramel and dark fruit.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Golden Promise in quantity, with crystal and a whisper of roasted barley.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Minimal English hops; bitterness is nearly absent by design.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Scottish ale yeast fermented cool to hold esters down at high gravity.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Some brewers add peated malt for light smoke; traditional versions do not.

composition.process: An extended boil caramelizes the wort into the toffee and plum core.

name: American Wild Ale
description: The American school of funk: brewers deploying Brettanomyces, Lactobacillus, and barrels with scientific abandon. Each release is a small ecosystem with a label on it.
funFact: Despite the name, most American 'wild' ales are carefully inoculated with lab-grown wild yeast strains — true spontaneous fermentation remains the rare exception.

serve.how: Stand the bottle upright for a day, then pour carefully into a tulip, stopping before the yeast sediment. Start cellar-cool and let it warm in the glass — funk, tart fruit, and oak reveal themselves in stages, so revisit the aroma every few minutes. Each bottle is its own little ecosystem: take small sips, and don't be surprised if the last glass tastes different from the first.

composition.summary: A base beer refermented with Brettanomyces and souring bacteria, usually in oak.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Varies by brewer; typically a pale or wheat base built for long aging.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Low and often aged — high alpha acids would inhibit the bacteria.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Brettanomyces plus Lactobacillus and Pediococcus over a clean primary.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Oak barrels or foeders house the microbes and add tannin and vanilla.

composition.process: Months to years of mixed-culture aging in wood, then blended across barrels.

name: Berliner Weisse
description: Berlin's featherweight sour wheat beer, tart as lemonade and barely stronger than kombucha. Locals famously tame it with a shot of raspberry or woodruff syrup.
funFact: Napoleon's troops occupying Berlin in the early 1800s are said to have dubbed it 'the Champagne of the North.'

serve.how: Pour chilled into a wide goblet and take it straight, at least at first — it's spritzy, lemony, and lighter than almost any beer you'll own. If the tartness is too sharp, do as Berliners do and add a small pour of raspberry or woodruff syrup to the glass ('mit Schuss'). At barely 3% it's a hot-afternoon beer: keep it cold, drink it fast, notice how the wheat softens the acid.

composition.summary: A low-gravity wheat and pilsner malt beer soured with Lactobacillus and barely hopped.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Roughly half wheat malt, half pilsner malt; nothing else needed.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Almost none — hop acids would kill the Lactobacillus.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Ale yeast alongside Lactobacillus; traditional versions also carry Brettanomyces.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Raspberry or woodruff syrup, added at the bar to tame the acidity.

composition.process: Co-fermented or kettle-soured with Lactobacillus, then packaged young and spritzy.

name: Catharina Sour
description: Brazil's signature sour: a light, quick-soured wheat beer flooded with fresh tropical fruit — passionfruit, guava, cajá. Sunshine engineered for 90-degree humidity.
funFact: Born in Santa Catarina state in the mid-2010s, it became one of the first Brazilian-born beer styles recognized in international style guidelines.

serve.how: Serve it cold in a tulip with an easy pour — the light wheat body doesn't need coaxing, and chill keeps the tartness bright and juicy. Get your nose in immediately: the fresh passionfruit and tropical aromatics are the style's signature and they're loudest right after the pour. Drink it young and fast like the Brazilian summer beer it is; this is not one to cellar.

composition.summary: A quick kettle-soured wheat beer refermented on fresh Brazilian tropical fruit.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pilsner malt with a large wheat portion for a soft, light body.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Essentially none; acidity and fruit carry the whole beer.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean ale yeast after the souring — no funk wanted here.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Fresh fruit: passionfruit, guava, cajá, jabuticaba, added after fermentation.

composition.process: Kettle souring with Lactobacillus, then a boil, fermentation, and a heavy fresh-fruit dose.

name: Faro
description: Lambic softened with candi sugar — the sweetened, sessionable form that once flowed as Brussels' everyday cheap beer. Now a rare sighting even in Belgium.
funFact: In 19th-century Brussels faro was the working class's daily drink, sometimes sweetened further at the table with sugar and a muddler.

serve.how: Pour it into a simple tumbler — no ceremony, this was Brussels' everyday café beer — and serve lightly chilled so the caramel sweetness and gentle tartness stay in balance. Notice the tug-of-war in every sip: candi-sugar toffee up front, soft lambic funk and acid underneath. It's the gentlest doorway into lambic there is, so share it with someone who thinks they hate sour beer.

composition.summary: Young lambic sweetened with candi or brown sugar and served fresh.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Lambic's base of pilsner malt and unmalted raw wheat.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Aged, oxidized hops used for preservation rather than bitterness.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: The spontaneous lambic culture: wild yeast, Brettanomyces, and bacteria.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Candi or brown sugar; historically it was added at the table.

composition.process: Blended young lambic is sweetened, then usually pasteurized so it cannot referment.

name: Flanders Red Ale
description: A sour red beer aged for up to two years in enormous oak vats until it tastes more like wine than beer. Cherry, balsamic, and oak in an unusually elegant package.
funFact: Its long maturation in giant oak foeders and vinous character earned it the nickname 'the Burgundy of Belgium.'

serve.how: Pour into a tulip at cellar temperature and treat it like a red wine: swirl, nose the cherry and balsamic, and give it ten minutes to open. Too cold and it's just sour; at 50°F+ the oak, toffee, and vinous fruit knit together into something elegant. Sip slowly and notice the balsamic tang playing off the malt sweetness — it pairs with food better than almost any beer made.

composition.summary: Vienna and caramel malts fermented with a mixed culture and aged years in oak.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Vienna and Munich malt with caramel malts for the deep red hue.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Aged hops at negligible bitterness.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Mixed culture of ale yeast, Lactobacillus, and acetic-leaning bacteria.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Enormous oak foeders host the fermentation and add tannin and vinous depth.

composition.process: Up to two years in oak, then blended with young beer to hit the house acidity.

name: Framboise
description: Raspberry lambic — perfumed, pink, and deceptively pretty for something born of wild fermentation. The friendliest ambassador the sour beer kingdom has ever sent out.
funFact: Raspberries joined the lambic tradition in the 20th century, well after cherries, and sweetened framboise became many drinkers' first-ever taste of wild beer.

serve.how: Chill it well and pour gently down the side of a flute to preserve the sparkle and show off the pink-ruby color. Nose it first — the raspberry perfume is half the pleasure — then sip and track the seesaw between fruit sweetness and lambic tartness. It doubles beautifully as an aperitif or a dessert pour; serve it where you'd otherwise open a sparkling rosé.

composition.summary: Lambic refermented on raspberries until the fruit's sugars are entirely gone.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pilsner malt with roughly a third unmalted raw wheat.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Aged hops for preservation only — no bitterness, no aroma.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Spontaneous wild culture: Brettanomyces, Lactobacillus, Pediococcus.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Raspberries added to the barrel; commercial versions are often back-sweetened.

composition.process: Fruit macerates in aged lambic for months, triggering a second fermentation.

name: Gose
description: A tart wheat beer seasoned with coriander and — improbably — salt. Nearly extinct by the late 20th century, it now thrives in craft taprooms like a rediscovered fossil species.
funFact: It is named after the river Gose in Goslar, and its salt and coriander survived the Reinheitsgebot purity law only because it was grandfathered in as a regional specialty.

serve.how: Pour chilled into a tall cylindrical gose glass — or any slender glass — with a soft head, and take your first sip without preconceptions. The salt shouldn't taste like seawater; it should just make the tart lemon and coriander pop, the way salt on the rim lifts a margarita. Notice how it makes your mouth water for the next sip: that saline snap is the whole trick of the style.

composition.summary: A wheat beer soured with Lactobacillus and seasoned with salt and coriander.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: About half wheat malt over a pilsner base.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Barely any — bitterness would fight the salt and the acid.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Ale yeast with Lactobacillus; historic versions used a mixed culture.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Salt and coriander seed are the style's defining additions.

composition.process: Kettle souring or mixed fermentation, with salt and coriander dosed for balance.

name: Gueuze
description: A blend of young and old lambics refermented in the bottle until fiercely carbonated and complex. Sour, funky, and cellar-worthy — the blender's art in liquid form.
funFact: Its vigorous bottle-fermentation and cork-and-cage presentation earned it the nickname 'Brussels Champagne.'

serve.how: Stand the bottle upright for at least a day, then uncork it like Champagne — point it away from anything you love, the carbonation is fierce. Pour slowly and steadily into a flute or tumbler in one motion, leaving the last ounce of sediment in the bottle. Sip at cellar-cool temperature and hunt through the layers: sharp green apple, barnyard funk, oak, and a sparkling dry finish that keeps evolving as it warms.

composition.summary: A blend of one-, two-, and three-year-old lambics refermented in the bottle.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pilsner malt with about a third unmalted raw wheat.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Aged, cheesy hops used purely as a preservative.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Spontaneous Zenne-valley culture: wild yeast, Brett, Lacto, Pedio.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Oak barrels shape both the fermentation and the funk.

composition.process: Young lambic's residual sugar feeds the bottle refermentation — no sugar is added.

name: Kettle Sour
description: The speedrun of sour brewing: wort is soured with Lactobacillus right in the kettle, then boiled clean and fermented normally. Tartness on a weekday timeline.
funFact: Kettle souring produces in a day or two the acidity that traditional lambic methods need one to three years to achieve — which is why taproom sours became suddenly ubiquitous in the 2010s.

serve.how: Serve it cold in a pint glass with a quick, easy pour — this is the approachable weekday sour, and chill keeps its clean tartness crisp and refreshing. Don't hunt for funk; unlike wild ales it's deliberately clean, so what you should notice is bright citrusy acidity over a light body. If it's a fruited version, swirl gently to wake the aroma and drink it fresh.

composition.summary: Ordinary wort soured with Lactobacillus in the kettle, then boiled and fermented clean.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Usually pilsner malt with wheat or oats for body.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Held back before souring, since hop acids inhibit Lactobacillus.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean ale yeast, pitched after the boil has killed the bacteria.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Fruit purée is a near-standard addition in modern taproom versions.

composition.process: Wort is held warm with Lactobacillus for a day or two, then boiled to lock in acidity.

name: Kriek
description: Lambic refermented on sour cherries, emerging ruby-red, tart, and faintly almondy from the pits. Fruit and funk locked in an elegant standoff.
funFact: Traditional versions use whole Schaarbeek sour cherries, pits and all — the pits contribute the style's subtle marzipan note.

serve.how: Pour gently down the side of a flute to keep the lively carbonation and admire the ruby glow before you drink. Nose it for sour cherry and a faint marzipan note from the pits, then sip and follow the dry, tart finish — a traditional kriek is fruit-forward but not sweet. Let it warm slightly toward 50°F and the earthy lambic underneath the cherries steps forward.

composition.summary: Lambic refermented on whole sour cherries, pits included.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pilsner malt with roughly a third unmalted raw wheat.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Aged hops for preservation; no perceptible bitterness.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Spontaneous wild culture of Brett, Lactobacillus, and Pediococcus.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Schaarbeek or Morello cherries — the pits give the almond note.

composition.process: Cherries macerate in aged lambic for months, then the beer is blended and bottled.

name: Lambic
description: Belgium's wild-fermented ancestor beer: the cooling wort is left open overnight so the native microbes of the Zenne valley can claim it. No two barrels ever turn out quite alike.
funFact: Lambic is fermented spontaneously in shallow open coolships and traditionally brewed only in the cooler months, when the wild airborne yeast is at its friendliest.

serve.how: Store the bottle upright for a day so the sediment settles, then pour gently into a tumbler in one steady motion, leaving the last half-inch of yeasty dregs behind. Traditional unblended lambic is nearly still, so don't chase a head — just let it breathe for a few minutes as it warms. Sip slowly and hunt for the layers: tart green apple up front, hay and oak in the middle, and that unmistakable barnyard funk on the long dry finish.

composition.summary: Pilsner malt and raw wheat, aged hops, and whatever wild yeast the night air brings.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Roughly two-thirds pilsner malt to one-third unmalted raw wheat.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Deliberately aged for years until they preserve without bittering.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Airborne wild yeast and bacteria: Brettanomyces, Lactobacillus, Pediococcus.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Oak barrels host years of slow fermentation and carry their own microflora.

composition.process: Hot wort cools overnight in an open coolship, is inoculated by the air, then barreled.

name: Oud Bruin
description: East Flanders' 'old brown' — a malty sour aged long and warm, then blended young into old like a solera. Darker, rounder, and less oaky than its red cousin to the west.
funFact: Unlike Flanders red, oud bruin traditionally sours during long aging in steel or lined tanks rather than oak, and blenders marry old and young batches to hit the house balance.

serve.how: Pour with moderate vigor down the center of a tulip to raise a tan collar of foam, then let it rest — this style opens up dramatically as the chill fades. Give the glass a gentle swirl between sips to release the raisin and caramel aromatics trapped under the sourness. Notice how the malty sweetness and gentle tartness trade places on your palate; the best examples balance them like sweet-and-sour sauce.

composition.summary: A dark Flemish malt grist fermented clean, then aged warm and blended for acidity.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Munich and pilsner malt with caramel and a little roasted malt.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Aged hops at minimal bitterness.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Ale yeast first, then Lactobacillus during the long warm maturation.

composition.process: Months of warm aging in steel or lined tanks, then old beer blended back into young.

name: Smoothie Sour
description: A kettle sour loaded with so much fruit purée it pours thick and opaque, often with lactose and vanilla riding along. Half beer, half dessert, entirely unsubtle.
funFact: Some smoothie sours contain so much fermentable fruit that breweries warn buyers to keep the cans cold — refermentation in the can has caused documented explosions and recalls.

serve.how: Keep the can refrigerated right up until serving — the fruit load in these can referment if left warm — and invert it gently once before opening to rouse the settled purée. Pour slowly into a teku; it will come out thick, opaque, and nearly headless, which is the style working as intended. Drink it fresh and cold like a dessert course, noticing how the sweet fruit hits first and the lactic tartness cuts through to keep it from cloying.

composition.summary: A kettle sour saturated with fruit purée, usually with lactose and vanilla riding along.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pilsner malt with heavy oats and wheat for a thick, opaque body.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: None to speak of.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean ale yeast pitched after the kettle souring.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Enormous fruit purée doses plus lactose and vanilla for dessert texture.

composition.process: Purée and lactose are blended in after fermentation, then the beer is packaged cold.

name: California Common
description: A Gold Rush survivor: lager yeast fermented warm in shallow vessels because ice was a luxury San Francisco didn't have. Toasty, minty, and proudly neither ale nor lager.
funFact: The traditional name 'steam beer' is a trademark of Anchor Brewing, which is why every other brewery must call the style California common.

serve.how: Pour briskly into a straight pint glass to build a sturdy off-white head — this style carries good carbonation and rewards a confident pour. Serve it a touch warmer than a standard lager so the toasted malt and woody, minty Northern Brewer hop character can show themselves. Take note of the odd, pleasing duality: crisp lager-like drinkability with a warm, toasty ale-ish middle.

composition.summary: Pale and crystal malt hopped with Northern Brewer, fermented warm using lager yeast.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Two-row pale malt with crystal for the toasty amber core.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Northern Brewer — the woody, minty signature of the style.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Lager yeast fermented at ale temperatures, giving a light fruitiness.

composition.process: Warm fermentation in wide, shallow vessels, historically to shed heat without ice.

name: Grodziskie
description: Poland's ghostly pale smoked wheat beer — light as a feather, fiercely carbonated, and made entirely from oak-smoked wheat malt. A style that died in the 1990s and clawed its way back.
funFact: Its brilliant clarity and champagne-level carbonation earned it the nickname 'Polish Champagne' before the last historic brewery closed in the 1990s; revivalists have since resurrected it.

serve.how: Pour slowly down the side of a tall flute — the champagne-level carbonation will whip up a huge white head if you rush it. Admire the brilliant pale clarity and the constant bead of bubbles rising like sparkling wine. Sip it spritzy and cold, noticing how the delicate oak smoke floats over the crisp wheat without any weight behind it; at around 3% ABV it is built for long, effortless sessions.

composition.summary: Made entirely from oak-smoked wheat malt, noble-hopped, and carbonated to champagne levels.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: One hundred percent oak-smoked wheat malt — no barley base at all.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Polish Lublin or German noble hops at surprisingly firm bitterness.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean ale yeast; historic versions used a house Polish strain.

composition.process: A protein-heavy all-wheat mash, then very high carbonation and clarification to brilliance.

name: Malt Liquor
description: An American lager bulked up with sugary adjuncts for extra strength at minimum cost, traditionally sold in 40-ounce bottles. The brash, misunderstood cousin of the lager family.
funFact: Despite the name, malt liquor contains no distilled liquor at all — it is simply an American legal term for lagers brewed above ordinary strength.

serve.how: This one wants to be as cold as your fridge can make it — warmth only amplifies the sweet grain and alcohol heat. Pour hard into a pint glass for a quick fluffy head, or honor tradition and drink it straight from the frosty 40. Drink it fast while the chill lasts, noticing the smooth corn sweetness up front and the warming finish that reminds you it punches above lager weight.

composition.summary: An American lager grist boosted with corn or sugar for extra alcohol.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: A modest six-row malt base doing the enzymatic work.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Barely present; bitterness is minimized to keep it easy.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Industrial lager yeast pushed to a higher-gravity finish.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Corn, rice, or dextrose supply cheap fermentable sugar and strength.

composition.process: A high-adjunct wort fermented out fully, sometimes with enzymes to squeeze out more alcohol.

name: Non-Alcoholic Lager
description: A lager with the alcohol carefully removed or never created, once a punchline and now a booming shelf category. The rare beer you can encounter before noon without judgment.
funFact: In Germany, non-alcoholic beer is marketed as an isotonic sports drink — Erdinger Alkoholfrei sponsors marathons and hands out cold ones at finish lines.

serve.how: Treat it exactly like a full-strength lager: pour down the middle of a tall pilsner glass to raise two fingers of white foam, which carries most of the aroma. Serve properly cold — NA beers can taste worty as they warm, so smaller pours kept cool beat one big glass going flat. Notice the clean grainy malt and crisp finish, and enjoy the novelty of a genuinely refreshing beer you can have with lunch on a Tuesday.

composition.summary: A normal pilsner grist whose alcohol is removed, or never fully created.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: German pilsner and Munich malt, exactly as in any ordinary lager.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Noble hops, often over-dosed to compensate for the lost body.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Standard lager yeast, or maltose-negative strains that barely ferment at all.

composition.process: Vacuum distillation, reverse osmosis, or arrested fermentation strips or prevents the alcohol.

name: Radler
description: Half lager, half lemon soda, all refreshment. Germany's official beverage of people who still have things to do this afternoon.
funFact: Radler means 'cyclist' — innkeeper Franz Xaver Kugler is credited with inventing it in 1922 by stretching his dwindling beer supply with lemon soda for a horde of thirsty cyclists.

serve.how: Serve it Bavarian-biergarten style: a chilled mug, a generous pour, and no ceremony whatsoever. If you're mixing your own, pour the lemon soda first and the lager second to keep the foam manageable, aiming for roughly half and half. Drink it fast and cold on a hot afternoon, enjoying how the sweet-tart lemon and light malt trade off — this is refreshment first, contemplation never.

composition.summary: Finished lager cut roughly half-and-half with lemon soda or lemonade.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Whatever helles or pilsner it's built on — pilsner malt base.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Low noble hopping; the citrus does the flavor work.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Standard lager yeast, from the base beer.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Lemon soda or lemonade, typically at a fifty-fifty ratio.

composition.process: Blended after the beer is already finished — no separate fermentation involved.

name: Rauchbier
description: Bamberg's smoked lager, brewed with malt dried over open beechwood fires. Tastes like a campfire learned excellent table manners.
funFact: Before modern kilns, virtually all malt was smoky — rauchbier is a living fossil, and Bamberg's Schlenkerla still smokes its own malt over beechwood logs.

serve.how: Pour into a stout seidel with a solid head and — crucially — let it warm out of the fridge for ten minutes; too cold and all you'll taste is smoke, too warm and it turns ashy. First sips can be startling, like drinking a campfire, so give your palate three or four swallows to recalibrate. Then notice the magic: the beechwood smoke and ham notes settle into a smooth, toasty Märzen backbone that keeps you coming back.

composition.summary: A märzen or helles grist using malt kilned over open beechwood fires.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Beechwood-smoked Munich malt, often half to all of the grist.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: German noble hops at low levels; the smoke does the talking.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Bavarian lager yeast fermented cold and clean.

components.label: Other
components.detail: The beechwood itself — Bamberg brewers still smoke their own malt.

composition.process: Malt is dried over open beech logs, then brewed as a standard cold-fermented lager.

name: Foreign Extra Stout
description: A robust export stout built to endure tropical shipping lanes, stronger and fruitier than the draught version. It found its truest home far from where it hatched.
funFact: Guinness Foreign Extra Stout descends from a 'West India Porter' first brewed in 1801, and Nigeria today buys more Guinness than Ireland does.

serve.how: Pour steadily into a tulip pint at a slight angle, straightening up at the end to crown it with a dense tan head. Serve warmer than fridge temperature — the dark fruit and vinous depth that separate this from a draught stout only emerge above 50°F. Sip slowly and track the arc from bittersweet chocolate through roast to that raisiny, almost port-like finish that made it a tropical legend.

composition.summary: A strong roasted-barley stout hopped hard for tropical export and fermented warm.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale malt with flaked barley and a heavy roasted barley charge.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: High bittering rates, historically for preservation on long voyages.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Vigorous ale yeast; some versions blend in a soured portion for tang.

composition.process: Fermented to high strength with heavy hopping so it survives heat and time.

name: Imperial Stout
description: A colossal dark-type brewed strong enough to survive frozen sea voyages to the Russian court. Dense with espresso, dark chocolate, and warming strength.
funFact: The 'imperial' title comes from the style's popularity at the court of Catherine the Great, to which London brewers exported it in the 1700s.

serve.how: Pour a modest measure into a snifter — this is a beer to treat like a fine spirit, not a pint. Cup the bowl in your palm to warm it, swirling occasionally to release waves of espresso, molasses, and dark chocolate as it opens up over half an hour. Share the bottle if it's a big one; the last warm sips are often the best, when the dried-fruit sweetness and warming alcohol fully unfold.

composition.summary: A massive grist of pale, roasted, and chocolate malts fermented to enormous strength.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale base with roasted barley, chocolate, and black malt in quantity.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Substantial bittering to keep all that sweetness in check.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: High-tolerance English or American ale yeast, pitched heavy.

composition.process: A long boil and a slow high-gravity fermentation, then months of conditioning.

name: Irish Dry Stout
description: A jet-black creature with a creamy white crown, roasty and surprisingly light on its feet. Its famous cascading pour is a nitrogen-powered special move.
funFact: The nitrogen pour that defines the modern pint was invented in 1959 by Michael Ash, a mathematician working for Guinness.

serve.how: If it's a nitro can or bottle, chill it, pour the whole thing hard into a tulip pint in one go, and then wait — let the famous cascade surge and settle into that dense ivory dome before you touch it. The proper two-part draught pour is worth imitating: patience is the ritual. Drink through the creamy head and notice how light-bodied it actually is beneath the roast and coffee — a 4% beer wearing a heavyweight's coat.

composition.summary: Pale malt, flaked barley, and roasted barley, hopped just enough to finish bone dry.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Irish pale malt with flaked barley and about ten percent roasted barley.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: English varieties at firm bitterness — East Kent Goldings or Target.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Irish ale yeast fermented warm and attenuated fully dry.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Nitrogen dispense: not an ingredient, but inseparable from the modern pint.

composition.process: Roasted barley, not chocolate malt, supplies the coffee bite and the dry finish.

name: Milk Stout
description: A sweet stout fortified with lactose, the milk sugar that yeast cannot digest. The result is a rounder, creamier beast than its dry Irish cousin.
funFact: Britain banned the name 'milk stout' in 1946 over fears it misled the public into thinking the beer contained actual milk.

serve.how: Pour at a 45-degree angle and finish upright to build a creamy tan head that mirrors the beer's texture. Serve it just off fridge-cold so the lactose sweetness and chocolate roundness aren't muted. Roll each sip across your tongue and notice the silky, almost café-au-lait body — the unfermentable milk sugar is doing exactly what the yeast couldn't touch.

composition.summary: A stout grist sweetened with lactose, a sugar brewer's yeast simply cannot ferment.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale malt with chocolate malt, roasted barley, and crystal.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Low bitterness so the sweetness reads creamy rather than cloying.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: English ale yeast, only moderately attenuative.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Lactose — milk sugar — added to the boil and left unfermented.

composition.process: Lactose goes in during the boil and survives fermentation intact, adding body and sweetness.

name: Oatmeal Stout
description: A stout given a silken texture by a dose of oats in the mash. Smooth and gently roasty, like breakfast reimagined by a brewer.
funFact: The style was nearly extinct until 1980, when Samuel Smith's brewed one at the request of an American importer after beer writer Michael Jackson lamented its disappearance.

serve.how: Pour with moderate vigor into a pint glass for a finger of dense, lasting foam. Let it lose its chill for a few minutes — the milk chocolate and nutty notes hide when it's too cold. The signature is texture, so pay attention to the mouthfeel: the oats give it a silky, pillowy slide that plain stouts can't match, making it dangerously easy drinking for something this roasty.

composition.summary: An English stout grist with flaked oats in the mash for a silken texture.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale malt, chocolate malt, roasted barley, and five to fifteen percent flaked oats.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: English hops at modest bitterness — Fuggle or Goldings.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: English ale yeast leaving a touch of residual sweetness.

composition.process: Oats in the mash contribute beta-glucans and lipids that give the beer its slick body.

name: Oyster Stout
description: A briny curiosity sometimes brewed with real oysters or their shells, which lend a subtle mineral snap. Its bond with shellfish dates to the Victorian pub table.
funFact: Stout and oysters were a classic Victorian pairing, but the first brewery known to put actual oysters in the brew did so in New Zealand in 1929.

serve.how: Pour into a pint glass with a steady hand, building a tan head, and serve just below cellar temperature. Sniff first for the faint sea-air minerality riding over the roast — it's subtle, more texture than taste. Best enjoyed the Victorian way: alongside a plate of oysters on the half shell, noticing how the briny snap in the beer bridges the roasted malt and the shellfish.

composition.summary: A dry stout brewed with whole oysters or their shells for a mineral brine.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale malt with flaked barley and roasted barley, as in any dry stout.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Modest English bittering; roast and brine lead instead.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: English or Irish ale yeast fermented warm.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Whole oysters or crushed shells add salinity and calcium.

composition.process: Oysters or shells go into the kettle, where the shells also help clarify the wort.

name: Pastry Stout
description: A dessert-mimic that disguises itself as cake, cookies, or pie using lactose, vanilla, and cacao. Sweetness levels can overwhelm unprepared trainers.
funFact: The term 'pastry stout' began as a half-insult on beer blogs in the late 2010s before brewers proudly adopted it as a badge.

serve.how: Pour a small measure into a snifter and treat it as dessert in a glass — a full pint of this is a commitment few finish gracefully. Let it warm and swirl gently; the vanilla, marshmallow, and chocolate-cake aromatics bloom as the chill fades. Sip slowly, splitting the bottle with a friend, and notice whether the roast underneath manages to hold the sweetness in check — that tension is the whole game.

composition.summary: An imperial stout loaded with lactose plus dessert adjuncts like vanilla and cacao.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: A big pale base with chocolate malt and roasted barley for structure.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Minimal — bitterness would only fight the sugar.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Ale yeast working through a high-gravity, high-sugar wort.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Lactose, vanilla beans, cacao nibs, maple, coconut, or marshmallow.

composition.process: Adjuncts are added after primary fermentation so sweetness and aroma survive to the can.

name: American Barleywine
description: The English barleywine's brash cousin, layering a wall of citrus-pine hops over immense malt. Hibernates well, its bitterness mellowing into marmalade over years.
funFact: Anchor Brewing's Old Foghorn, first brewed in 1975, is regarded as the first modern American barleywine.

serve.how: Pour gently into a snifter, leaving any sediment in the bottle, and give it time — this beer changes more in the glass than almost any other. Warm it in your palm and swirl to pull up the pine and candied-orange hop aromas over the caramel base. If you have two bottles, cellar one for a year or three and taste how the sharp bitterness relaxes into marmalade; either way, sip it like an after-dinner drink, never in a hurry.

composition.summary: A huge pale malt bill buried under aggressive American hop bitterness and aroma.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Two-row pale in quantity with crystal malt for caramel depth.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Big Cascade, Centennial, and Chinook charges — citrus and pine at high IBUs.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: High-alcohol-tolerant American ale yeast, pitched heavy.

composition.process: A long boil for caramelization, then slow high-gravity fermentation and heavy dry hopping.

name: English Barleywine
description: A legendary sipping beast, dark with toffee and dried fruit, that improves for years in the cellar. Wine-strength, but unmistakably ale at heart.
funFact: Bass No. 1 is generally credited as the first beer marketed as a 'barley wine,' back in Victorian England.

serve.temp: 55-62°F, cellar temp or just below room temp
serve.how: Decant carefully into a snifter, holding back the sediment if it's a bottle-conditioned or aged example, and pour only a few ounces at a time. This is a fireside sipper: cradle the glass, swirl, and let the toffee, fig, and sherry notes unfold over a long evening. Notice the vinous, leathery depth that comes with age — a well-cellared bottle drinks closer to a tawny port than a pint.

composition.summary: An enormous English malt bill, boiled long, fermented slow, and cellared for years.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Maris Otter in huge quantity with crystal and a touch of dark malt.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: English varieties at high kettle rates; the aroma fades with age.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: English ale yeast pitched heavy and stepped up over a slow fermentation.

composition.process: A very long boil caramelizes the wort, then years of cellaring build sherry and leather.

name: Old Ale
description: An ancient English keeper-beer, aged until it develops dark fruit, leather, and a whisper of pleasant funk. A living fossil of pre-industrial brewing.
funFact: These beers were historically matured in wooden vats for months or years, and drinkers prized the aged character they called 'stale' as a compliment.

serve.how: Let the bottle stand upright before opening, then pour slowly into a snifter, leaving the last swirl of sediment behind. Serve at true cellar temperature and resist rushing — the raisin, molasses, and leather notes need warmth and air to speak. Search each sip for the whisper of tart, aged 'stale' character that old-school drinkers prized; it should read as complexity, not flaw.

composition.summary: A strong English malt beer matured until it develops dark fruit and gentle funk.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale malt with crystal, brown malt, and sometimes molasses-dark specialty malts.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: English hops at moderate levels; the bitterness softens over aging.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: English ale yeast, often joined by Brettanomyces during the long maturation.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Wooden vats contribute oxidative sherry notes and a light tartness.

composition.process: Months or years of vat aging, historically blended with fresh beer before serving.

name: American Wheat Beer
description: A wheat beer run through a clean American filter: no banana, no clove, just soft grain and citrusy hops. The approachable gateway creature of many a craft taproom.
funFact: The style took off in 1980s Portland when Widmer Brothers brewed an American 'hefeweizen' with clean yeast — accidentally defining a new, banana-free category.

serve.how: Pour down the middle of a pint glass to raise a fluffy white head — the wheat protein gives it great foam, so use it. Skip the fruit garnish; a clean example doesn't need one. Drink it cold and easy, noticing the soft grainy middle and the light citrusy hop finish where a German wheat would put banana and clove — the whole point is crisp, no-drama refreshment.
