composition.process: The living flor blanket seals the wine from air while eating its glycerin and sugar, leaving it lean and saline.

name: Manzanilla Sherry
description: Fino's coastal cousin, aged only in one seaside town where ocean air keeps its yeast blanket thriving. Drinkers swear they taste salt spray and chamomile in every sip.
funFact: Manzanilla may only be aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, where humid Atlantic air keeps the flor yeast alive and vigorous year-round.

serve.how: Pour it well chilled into a copita and drink it fresh — buy small bottles and finish them within days, as its delicate coastal character fades fast once open. Serve as the opening act of a meal with salty snacks in hand. Notice the seaside signature: chamomile and green olive over an almost briny, sea-salt finish.

composition.summary: Palomino aged under flor exclusively in the seaside town of Sanlúcar de Barrameda.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Palomino Fino, from the same albariza vineyards as fino

components.label: Region
components.detail: Sanlúcar de Barrameda only, at the mouth of the Guadalquivir

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Fortified low; humid Atlantic air keeps flor thick year-round

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Solera aging in coastal bodegas built with high, ventilated walls

composition.process: Sanlúcar's damp ocean air feeds a heavier, more persistent flor than inland Jerez, which is why it tastes of salt spray.

name: Oloroso Sherry
description: Fortified high from the start so no yeast can shield it, this sherry ages in open combat with oxygen. Decades later it emerges dark, walnut-rich, and structurally imposing.
funFact: Oloroso means 'fragrant' in Spanish; the style is fortified above 17% precisely so that flor yeast cannot survive on its surface.

serve.how: Serve at cool room temperature in a copita — chilling too hard mutes its walnut-and-leather depth. Pour a couple of ounces, swirl generously, and sip it like you would an aged whisky; an open bottle holds for a month or more. Notice the paradox of a dry sherry that smells sweet: all that toffee and dried fruit on the nose resolves into a savory, structured palate.

composition.summary: Palomino fortified high enough to kill flor, then aged openly against oxygen.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Palomino Fino, from the albariza chalk of Jerez

components.label: Region
components.detail: Jerez de la Frontera, Andalucía, Spain

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Fortified above 17% from the start, so flor never forms

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Decades of oxidative solera aging; the wine concentrates as it evaporates

composition.process: Fortifying past 17% at the outset denies flor any chance to grow, committing the wine to a life of oxidation.

name: Palo Cortado Sherry
description: The bodega's happy accident: a wine that set out to become fino but lost its flor and drifted toward oloroso richness. It keeps amontillado's finesse and oloroso's body.
funFact: Its name means 'cut stick,' after the chalk mark cellar masters slash across casks whose flor has unexpectedly died, rerouting the wine to oxidative aging.

serve.how: Serve just cool in a copita and give it a real swirl — this rarity carries amontillado's aromatic finesse on oloroso's rich frame, and both deserve airtime. Pour small, sip slow, and revisit as it warms in the glass. Track the shape-shift from bright citrus peel and sea salt into hazelnut and toffee on the long finish.

composition.summary: Palomino that began as fino, lost its flor unexpectedly, and turned oxidative.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Palomino Fino, selected from the finest albariza parcels

components.label: Region
components.detail: Jerez de la Frontera and El Puerto de Santa María

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Flor dies unbidden; the cask is refortified and rerouted

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Long oxidative solera aging, often decades in the bodega

composition.process: A cellar master chalks a cut mark on the butt whose flor has failed, sending it down the oxidative path.

name: Pedro Ximénez Sherry
description: Grapes sun-dried to near-raisins before pressing yield a black, syrupy elixir of fig and molasses. Less a beverage than a dessert that happens to pour.
funFact: PX can exceed 400 grams of sugar per liter, and in Spain it is famously poured straight over vanilla ice cream.

serve.how: Serve small, slightly cool pours in a copita — an ounce or two is dessert in itself — or go full Spanish and pour it straight over vanilla ice cream. Swirl and watch the black syrup coat the glass in slow legs. Sip in tiny amounts and let fig, molasses, and espresso saturate the palate; a bottle lasts for months in the fridge.

composition.summary: Pedro Ximénez grapes sun-dried to raisins, pressed into black syrup in Andalucía.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Pedro Ximénez, much of it grown in neighbouring Montilla-Moriles

components.label: Region
components.detail: Jerez, with fruit historically dried in Montilla-Moriles

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Grapes sun-dried on esparto mats, pressed, then muted with spirit

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Solera aging in old butts, deepening to opaque black

composition.process: Spirit is added almost immediately to stop fermentation, preserving nearly all the raisined sugar in the pressed juice.

name: Orange Wine
description: White wine made like a red: the juice ferments on its grape skins for days or months, emerging amber-hued, tannic, and faintly wild. Contains no oranges whatsoever.
funFact: The technique traces back roughly 8,000 years to Georgia, where wine is still fermented in buried clay vessels called qvevri — a method inscribed on UNESCO's cultural heritage list.

serve.how: Serve cooler than a red but warmer than a white — over-chilling buries its wild aromatics and accentuates the tannin. Pour into a white wine glass, swirl, and give it a few minutes; some bottles are unfiltered, so stand them upright beforehand and expect a little haze. Taste it like a red in white's clothing: dried apricot and black tea with a grippy, savory finish that loves food.

composition.summary: White grapes fermented on their skins — Rkatsiteli in Georgia, Ribolla Gialla in Friuli.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: White varieties: Rkatsiteli in Georgia, Ribolla Gialla and Pinot Grigio elsewhere

components.label: Region
components.detail: Georgia's Kakheti heartland; also Friuli, Slovenia and beyond

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Skin and stem contact for days to months, like a red

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Buried qvevri clay amphorae in Georgia; neutral wood elsewhere

composition.process: Fermenting white juice on its skins extracts tannin and phenolic color, producing amber wine with a red wine's grip.

name: Cava
description: Spain's bottle-fermented answer to Champagne, made mostly in Catalonia from a trio of local grapes. Delivers toasty traditional-method character at a friendly price.
funFact: The name simply means 'cellar' in Catalan, after the underground caves where the bottles age; the classic blend is Macabeo, Xarel·lo, and Parellada.

serve.how: Chill thoroughly, then open with a whisper, not a pop — ease the cork out while holding it, keeping the bottle at 45 degrees. Pour slowly down the side of a tulip glass to preserve the mousse. Watch the bead, then taste for quince and citrus with the almond-and-toast signature of real bottle fermentation at a fraction of Champagne's price — which makes it guilt-free for weeknight tapas.

composition.summary: Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada, bottle-fermented in the cellars of Catalonia's Penedès.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada; Chardonnay and Trepat also permitted

components.label: Region
components.detail: Penedès in Catalonia supplies the overwhelming majority

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Traditional method: second fermentation inside each individual bottle

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Min. 9 months on lees; Reserva 18, Gran Reserva 30

composition.process: A second fermentation sealed inside the bottle traps the bubbles and leaves spent yeast to build toasty complexity.

name: Champagne
description: The apex predator of sparkling wine, born of a second fermentation inside each bottle in France's chilly northeast. Its very name is guarded by law worldwide.
funFact: The pressure inside a Champagne bottle reaches about six atmospheres — roughly triple the pressure in a car tire.

serve.how: Chill three hours in the fridge or 30 minutes in an ice-water bucket, then twist the bottle — not the cork — until it releases with a soft sigh; six atmospheres of pressure deserve respect. Pour gently down the tilted side of a tulip glass, which shows more aroma than a skinny flute. Watch the endless bead of tiny bubbles, and taste for brioche and green apple with that chalky mineral snap on the finish.
pair: salty potato chips with crème fraîche

composition.summary: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier, bottle-fermented on the chalk of northeast France.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier, in almost any proportion

components.label: Region
components.detail: Champagne AOC: Montagne de Reims, Côte des Blancs, Vallée de la Marne

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Méthode traditionnelle: tirage, riddling, disgorgement, then a dosage

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Non-vintage at least 15 months; vintage bottlings three years

composition.process: Yeast and sugar sealed into each bottle ferment a second time, dissolving CO2 to roughly six atmospheres of pressure.

name: Crémant
description: France's family of traditional-method sparklers made everywhere except Champagne — Alsace, the Loire, Burgundy, and beyond. The insider's route to fine French bubbles.
funFact: There are eight Crémant appellations across France, from Crémant d'Alsace to Crémant de Limoux, all using Champagne's bottle-fermentation method.

serve.how: Chill the bottle for at least three hours, ease the cork out with a sigh rather than a pop, and pour slowly down the tilted side of a tulip glass to preserve the mousse. Let it sit a moment so the foam settles, then top up to about two-thirds full. Notice how the apple and citrus up front give way to a brioche note from its Champagne-method lees aging — proof you got fine French bubbles at half the price.

composition.summary: Traditional-method French sparkling wine from eight appellations outside Champagne.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Local varieties: Chenin in the Loire, Pinot Blanc in Alsace, Mauzac at Limoux

components.label: Region
components.detail: Eight appellations: Alsace, Loire, Bourgogne, Limoux, Bordeaux, Jura, Die, Savoie

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Same bottle-fermentation as Champagne, with hand-harvest and whole-bunch pressing required

components.label: Aging
components.detail: At least nine months on the lees before disgorgement

composition.process: The Champagne method applied to regional grapes — same second fermentation in bottle, different fruit and a lower price.

name: English Sparkling Wine
description: A cool-climate upstart from the chalk hills of southern England that has taken to beating Champagne in blind tastings. Crisp, taut, and quietly smug about the whole thing.
funFact: The chalk downs of southern England belong to the same geological basin as the chalk beneath Champagne, just across the Channel.

serve.how: Treat it exactly like good Champagne: a long fridge chill, a gentle quarter-twist of the bottle while holding the cork still, and a slow pour into a tulip glass. Don't serve it ice-cold from a bucket — a few degrees warmer lets the chalk and brioche notes emerge behind the green apple snap. Sip slowly and watch the fine, persistent bead; that taut, mouthwatering acidity is the signature of England's cool chalk hills.

composition.summary: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier grown on the chalk downs of southern England.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier; the Champagne trio exactly

components.label: Region
components.detail: Sussex, Kent and Hampshire, on southern England's chalk

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Traditional method, with second fermentation and riddling in bottle

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Extended lees aging, typically well past Champagne's minimums

composition.process: A marginally cool climate on the same chalk seam as Champagne yields the searing acidity that bottle aging then rounds out.

name: Franciacorta
description: Italy's most serious sparkling wine, bottle-fermented in Lombardy from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. It rarely leaves Italy, where locals happily drink most of it themselves.
funFact: Non-vintage Franciacorta must age at least 18 months on its lees in bottle — longer than the 12 months required for non-vintage Champagne.

serve.how: Serve this slightly warmer than everyday fizz — its long lees aging deserves room to speak. Pour gently into a tulip glass, give it a minute to open, and take a slow first sip before the chill fully lifts. Look for the baked apple and hazelnut richness layered over citrus; that toasty depth is what 18-plus months on the lees buys you.

composition.summary: Chardonnay and Pinot Nero, bottle-fermented in Lombardy near Lake Iseo.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Chardonnay and Pinot Nero, plus Pinot Bianco and native Erbamat

components.label: Region
components.detail: Franciacorta DOCG, on glacial moraine south of Lake Iseo

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Metodo classico: second fermentation and riddling in bottle

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Non-vintage rests at least 18 months on its lees

composition.process: Italy's longest mandatory lees aging for a non-vintage sparkler is what gives Franciacorta its bready depth.

name: Lambrusco
description: A frothing purple sparkler from Emilia-Romagna, engineered by generations of Italians to cut through plates of salumi and lasagna. Dry versions bear no resemblance to its sugary 1980s reputation.
funFact: In the late 1970s and 1980s, sweet Lambrusco was the best-selling imported wine in the United States.

serve.how: Chill it like a white wine, then pour a generous measure into a white wine glass — no flute needed, the froth is meant to relax into a purple foam and fade. Seek out a bottle labeled secco (dry) and forget the sugary 1980s versions. Sip it alongside rich, fatty food and notice how the blackberry fruit and gentle fizz scrub your palate clean between bites.

composition.summary: Several distinct Lambrusco grape varieties, fizzed up across Emilia-Romagna.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Lambrusco Grasparossa, Salamino, Sorbara and Maestri — genuinely different varieties

components.label: Region
components.detail: Emilia-Romagna, around Modena and Reggio Emilia

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Charmat tank fermentation mostly; some producers use the ancestral method

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; bottled young while the purple froth is at its brightest

composition.process: A second fermentation in pressurized tank keeps the fruit fresh and the foam abundant, ready to cut through salumi.

name: Pét-Nat
description: Short for pétillant naturel: wine bottled before its first fermentation finishes, trapping bubbles the ancestral way. Often cloudy, usually crown-capped, always a little unpredictable.
funFact: The ancestral method behind pét-nat predates Champagne's technique — monks at Saint-Hilaire near Limoux were making sparkling wine this way in the 1500s.

serve.how: Chill it upright for a day so the sediment settles, then pop the crown cap over the sink — pét-nat can be lively. Pour the first glasses gently off the sediment, or give the bottle a slow roll first if you want the cloudy, yeasty full experience; both are legitimate. Expect orchard fruit and a little funk rather than polish, and drink it young and cold — unpredictability is the charm.

composition.summary: Any grape bottled mid-fermentation — the ancestral method, older than Champagne.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Anything: Mauzac at Limoux, Chenin, Gamay, Glera, whatever the grower has

components.label: Region
components.detail: Limoux is the ancestral home; now made worldwide

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Méthode ancestrale: bottled before the first fermentation finishes

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; usually undisgorged, cloudy, and sealed with a crown cap

composition.process: The first and only fermentation finishes inside the sealed bottle, so the bubbles are the wine's original carbon dioxide.

name: Prosecco
description: Italy's cheerful, pear-scented fizz, made from the Glera grape and carbonated in big steel tanks rather than bottles. The engine behind every Aperol Spritz.
funFact: Prosecco takes its name from a small village near Trieste, though most of it now comes from vineyards between Conegliano and Valdobbiadene.

serve.how: Prosecco wants to be cold — give it a proper fridge chill or twenty minutes in an ice bucket before opening. Pour down the side of a tulip glass and drink it fresh and young; its pear-and-white-flower charm fades fast in an open bottle. Enjoy it as an aperitivo on its own, and save any leftovers for tomorrow's Aperol Spritz or mimosa.

composition.summary: The Glera grape, fermented sparkling in steel tanks across northeastern Italy.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Glera predominantly, with Verdiso, Bianchetta and Perera permitted in support

components.label: Region
components.detail: Conegliano Valdobbiadene DOCG and the broader Prosecco DOC, Veneto

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Charmat method: second fermentation in a large pressurized tank

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; tank fermentation and quick bottling preserve pear and white flower

composition.process: Tank fermentation keeps the wine off spent yeast, which is exactly why it tastes of fresh fruit rather than bread.

name: Sekt
description: Germany's homegrown sparkler, at its best when made from Riesling with racy acidity and orchard fruit. Most of it never escapes the German-speaking world.
funFact: Germans are among the world's biggest per-capita drinkers of sparkling wine, which explains why so little Sekt is left over to export.

serve.how: Hunt down a Riesling-based Winzersekt (grower Sekt) and chill it well before easing the cork out quietly. Pour into a tulip glass and let the racy acidity lead — this is orchard fruit and mineral zip rather than toasty richness. Notice the green apple and white peach snap; it drinks beautifully as an aperitif and keeps its nerve right through dinner.

composition.summary: German sparkling wine, at its best from Riesling grown along the Rhine and Mosel.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Riesling for the serious bottles; Pinot Blanc, Elbling and Pinot Noir too

components.label: Region
components.detail: Germany; Mosel, Rheingau and Pfalz for estate-grown Winzersekt

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Mostly tank method; Winzersekt uses bottle fermentation from estate fruit

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Basic Sekt released quickly; Winzersekt rests months on its lees

composition.process: The best examples take Riesling's racy acidity through a bottle fermentation, giving orchard fruit real backbone.

name: Dry Vermouth
description: The pale, herbal French counterpart to Italy's sweet style, crisp with alpine botanicals and citrus. Best known as the whispering partner in a Martini.
funFact: The dry French style was developed around 1813 by Joseph Noilly, whose Noilly Prat remains the benchmark bartenders reach for in a classic Martini.

serve.how: Vermouth is wine, so keep the open bottle in the refrigerator and finish it within a month or two. Pour a small measure into a chilled small wine glass — no ice needed if the bottle is cold — and add a twist of lemon peel, expressing the oils over the surface. Sip it slowly as an aperitif and pick out the chamomile and alpine herbs that usually hide inside your Martini.

composition.summary: Neutral white wine from southern France, fortified and steeped with alpine botanicals.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Neutral whites: Clairette, Piquepoul and Ugni Blanc in the French style

components.label: Region
components.detail: Marseillan and the Lyon region; the French dry tradition

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Wine fortified, then infused with wormwood, chamomile and citrus peel

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Noilly Prat weathers its base wine outdoors in oak for a year

composition.process: Leaving the base wine exposed to sun, wind and sea air oxidizes it before the botanicals ever go in.

name: Sweet Vermouth
description: Wine aromatized with wormwood, spices, and bittersweet botanicals in the Italian style. Equally content stirred into a Negroni or served alone over ice with an orange slice, as Turin intended.
funFact: Modern sweet vermouth was born in Turin in 1786 at the shop of Antonio Benedetto Carpano, and the word 'vermouth' comes from 'Wermut,' German for wormwood.

serve.temp: Chilled bottle, served over one large cube
serve.how: Do it as Turin intended: pour two to three ounces over a large ice cube in a rocks glass and garnish with a fat orange slice or expressed peel. A splash of soda turns it into a proper low-proof aperitivo highball if you like. Sip slowly and trace the bitter orange, clove, and cola notes as the ice slowly opens it up — and keep the bottle in the fridge once opened.

composition.summary: Neutral white wine, fortified and aromatized with wormwood, spices and caramel in Turin.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Neutral white base wine; the red color comes from caramel, not grapes

components.label: Region
components.detail: Turin and Piedmont, home of the Italian rosso style

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Fortified, infused with wormwood and spices, sweetened with sugar

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Little or none; house botanical recipes matter more than time

composition.process: Wormwood — Wermut in German, hence the name — is macerated with dozens of spices to build a bittersweet profile.

name: Albariño
description: A saline, citrusy coastal dweller from Spain's rainy northwest, seemingly engineered by nature to accompany shellfish. Often carries a whisper of sea spray.
funFact: Across the border in Portugal the same grape is called Alvarinho, where it stars in the finest bottlings of Vinho Verde.

serve.how: Chill it down, pour a modest measure into a white wine glass, and let it warm slightly in the glass rather than over-icing the bottle. Give it a quick swirl and look for the whisper of sea spray behind the lemon zest and white peach. It is at its absolute best alongside shellfish — drink it the way they do in Galicia, with something briny on the table.

composition.summary: Albariño from the rainy Atlantic coast of Rías Baixas in Galicia.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Albariño; the same grape as Portugal's Alvarinho across the Minho

components.label: Region
components.detail: Rías Baixas, Galicia, especially Val do Salnés on granite

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool stainless fermentation; some producers age on fine lees

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rarely oaked; most is bottled young and drunk younger

composition.process: Cool fermentation in steel preserves the thick-skinned grape's citrus aromatics and that whisper of Atlantic salt.

name: Assyrtiko
description: A volcanic survivor from Santorini that keeps razor acidity even under scorching Aegean sun. Bone dry, smoky, and startlingly saline.
funFact: On windswept Santorini, Assyrtiko vines are woven into low basket shapes called kouloura, with the grapes growing inside for protection.

serve.how: Serve it a touch warmer than a simple summer white — too cold and you mute the smoke and beeswax that make it special. Pour, swirl, and take a moment with the nose: flint and salt first, then lemon underneath. Its razor acidity begs for food, so treat it like a serious dry white and drink it through a meal rather than before one.

composition.summary: Assyrtiko grown on Santorini's volcanic ash, on ungrafted, basket-trained vines.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Assyrtiko; vines ungrafted, phylloxera never survived the volcanic soil

components.label: Region
components.detail: Santorini, in the Aegean; also mainland Greek plantings

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Fermented dry in steel; the barrel-aged version is called Nykteri

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Mostly none; Nykteri and top cuvées see oak and time

composition.process: Vines woven into low kouloura baskets shelter the fruit from Aegean wind, so acidity survives ferocious sun.

name: Chablis
description: Chardonnay stripped to its skeleton: steely, saline, and rarely troubled by oak. It grows in cold northern Burgundy atop ancient seabed.
funFact: Chablis vines grow in Kimmeridgian limestone studded with fossilized oyster shells from a sea that covered the region 150 million years ago.

serve.how: Resist the ice bucket — over-chilled Chablis tastes like cold water, while at cellar-cool temperature the oyster-shell and flint notes come alive. Pour into a white wine glass, swirl gently, and let it sit ten minutes if it seems shy. Taste for the steely, saline finish; this is Chardonnay with its makeup off, and premier cru bottles reward slow, attentive sipping.
pair: sole or other delicate white fish

composition.summary: Pure Chardonnay grown on Kimmeridgian limestone in the cold north of Burgundy.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Chardonnay only, with no other variety permitted

components.label: Region
components.detail: Chablis, northern Burgundy, on fossil-studded Kimmeridgian limestone

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Steel or neutral wood; oak is deliberately kept off the fruit

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Village wines see steel; Grand Crus may rest in old barrels

composition.process: Refusing new oak leaves nothing between you and the cold-climate acidity and oyster-shell minerality of the site.

name: Chardonnay
description: The great shape-shifter of white grapes, appearing lean and steely in cool cellars yet golden and buttery wherever oak barrels lurk. Found on virtually every wine list on Earth.
funFact: DNA analysis at UC Davis revealed Chardonnay is a natural cross between noble Pinot Noir and the humble medieval grape Gouais Blanc.

serve.temp: 48-55°F — cooler for unoaked, warmer for oaked
serve.how: Match the chill to the style: lean, unoaked bottles want a proper fridge chill, while rich, barrel-aged versions show best only lightly cooled so the butter and vanilla can unfurl. Pour into a generous white wine glass and swirl well — oaked Chardonnay especially rewards aeration. Notice whether you get green apple and citrus (steel) or toast and vanilla (oak); it's the same grape playing two different characters.

composition.summary: Chardonnay, a Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc cross, born in Burgundy and grown everywhere.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Chardonnay; a natural cross of Pinot Noir and Gouais Blanc

components.label: Region
components.detail: Côte de Beaune and Mâconnais in Burgundy; now every wine country

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Barrel fermentation, lees stirring and malolactic build the buttery style

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Anywhere from steel-only to a year in new French oak

composition.process: Malolactic fermentation generates diacetyl — the same compound in butter — which is where the 'buttery' Chardonnay comes from.

name: Chenin Blanc
description: The Loire's do-everything grape, capable of dry, sweet, still, and sparkling forms without breaking a sweat. Its searing acidity lets great examples age for half a century.
funFact: South Africa grows more Chenin Blanc than France does, where the grape has long gone by the local name 'Steen'.

serve.how: Check the style before you pour — Chenin runs from bone dry to honeyed, and drier versions take more chill than sweeter ones. Serve in a white wine glass, swirl, and hunt for the grape's odd, wonderful signature: quince and honey with a lanolin, wet-wool undertone. Its searing acidity keeps even off-dry bottles fresh, so if you own an aged Vouvray, give it a few minutes of air and sip patiently.

composition.summary: Chenin Blanc from the middle Loire, made dry, sweet, still or sparkling.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Chenin Blanc; known as Steen across South Africa

components.label: Region
components.detail: Vouvray, Savennières, Montlouis and Anjou in the Loire Valley

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Sec to moelleux; botrytis for sweet, traditional method for sparkling

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Old barrels or steel; great examples last half a century

composition.process: Its extraordinary natural acidity lets a grower stop fermentation anywhere on the sugar scale and still make a balanced wine.

name: Gewürztraminer
description: An unmistakably perfumed specimen that smells of lychee and rose petals before you even lift the glass. Loud, golden, and impossible to confuse with anything else.
funFact: The grape takes its name from the village of Tramin in the Italian Alps, with 'Gewürz' meaning 'spice' in German.

serve.how: Don't over-chill it — this grape's whole point is perfume, and cold smothers it. Pour a smaller measure than usual into a white wine glass (it's rich and often high in alcohol), then smell before you sip: lychee and rose petal should leap out before the glass reaches your lips. On the palate, notice the oily, golden texture and ginger spice; it's a wine you sip, not gulp.

composition.summary: Gewürztraminer, a pink-skinned Traminer mutation named for the village of Tramin.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Gewürztraminer, an aromatic pink-skinned mutation of Traminer

components.label: Region
components.detail: Alsace above all; Alto Adige, Germany and New Zealand too

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Slow pressing of pink skins; often finished with a little sugar

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually none; large neutral casks in Alsace, never new oak

composition.process: Its skins are loaded with terpenes — the same aromatic compounds in rose petals and lychee — which pressing coaxes out.

name: Grüner Veltliner
description: Austria's signature white, zippy and green-tinged with a telltale flick of white pepper on the finish. A sommelier favorite for its uncanny food friendliness.
funFact: Its peppery bite comes from rotundone, the same aroma compound found in actual black peppercorns and in Syrah.

serve.how: Serve it fridge-cool in a white wine glass and pour freely — this is Austria's great table wine, built for drinking with food. Swirl and sniff for the telltale flick of white pepper over green apple and lime. It's famously the sommelier's escape hatch for hard-to-pair plates, so test it against vegetables that normally wreck wine, like asparagus or artichokes.

composition.summary: Grüner Veltliner from the terraced Danube valleys of Lower Austria.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Grüner Veltliner, Austria's most planted variety by a distance

components.label: Region
components.detail: Wachau, Kremstal, Kamptal and the Weinviertel, in Lower Austria

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool steel fermentation; oak is used sparingly if at all

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Fresh Steinfeder and Federspiel young; ripe Smaragd rewards years

composition.process: Clean steel fermentation preserves rotundone, the peppercorn compound that gives the wine its unmistakable green-pepper flick.

name: Muscadet
description: A briny, feather-light white from the Atlantic mouth of the Loire, made from the Melon de Bourgogne grape. It exists in near-perfect symbiosis with raw oysters.
funFact: Bottles labeled 'sur lie' rest on their spent yeast cells through the winter, picking up a subtle creaminess and a faint natural spritz.

serve.how: Chill it hard and pour it cold — Muscadet is a featherweight built for refreshment, not contemplation. Look for 'sur lie' on the label and notice the subtle creaminess and faint prickle it picks up from a winter resting on its yeast. The wine is almost neutral on its own; put a plate of raw oysters next to it and the briny, lemony pairing suddenly makes perfect sense.

composition.summary: Melon de Bourgogne from the Atlantic mouth of the Loire, aged on its lees.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Melon de Bourgogne, a Burgundian exile now unique to Nantes

components.label: Region
components.detail: Sèvre et Maine in the Pays Nantais, at the Loire's mouth

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Fermented dry in tank or underground glass-lined vats

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 'Sur lie' bottlings rest on spent yeast through the winter

composition.process: Bottling straight off the lees without racking adds a creamy texture and faint prickle to an otherwise austere wine.

name: Picpoul de Pinet
description: A zesty Mediterranean white from the lagoons of the Languedoc, traditionally shipped in a distinctive tall green bottle. Built for oysters farmed within sight of its vines.
funFact: The grape's name, Piquepoul, translates roughly to 'lip stinger' — a nod to its bracing acidity.

serve.how: Serve it cold from the fridge in a white wine glass and don't overthink it — the tall green bottle is a promise of simple seaside pleasure. Take a sip and feel the 'lip-stinger' acidity that gives the grape its name, chased by lemon and a saline snap. It's the house pour of the Languedoc's oyster farms, so drink it with anything briny, fried, or fresh off the grill.

composition.summary: Piquepoul Blanc grown beside the oyster lagoons of the Languedoc coast.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Piquepoul Blanc; the name means roughly 'lip stinger'

components.label: Region
components.detail: Pinet and neighbouring villages beside the Étang de Thau, Languedoc

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Picked early and fermented cold to protect its bracing acidity

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; steel only, shipped in its tall green bottle

composition.process: Early picking in a hot Mediterranean region is the whole trick — it keeps the acid that oysters demand.

name: Pinot Grigio
description: A light, breezy sipper that evolved from a grayish-pink mutation of Pinot Noir. In its Italian form it is crisp and neutral; as Alsatian Pinot Gris it grows richer and spicier.
funFact: Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are the exact same grape — the 'gris' (gray) refers to the oddly grayish-blue tint of its skins.

serve.how: Chill it properly and pour into a white wine glass; Italian-style Pinot Grigio is about crisp refreshment, so drink it young and cold. Swirl lightly and look for pear, lemon, and a faint almond bitterness on the finish. If your bottle is a richer Alsatian Pinot Gris, serve it a few degrees warmer to let its spice and weight show.

composition.summary: Pinot Gris, a grey-skinned Pinot Noir mutation, crisp in Italy and richer in Alsace.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Pinot Gris; a color mutation of Pinot Noir with greyish skins

components.label: Region
components.detail: Veneto, Friuli and Alto Adige in Italy; Alsace in France

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Pressed fast off pink skins in Italy; riper and fuller in Alsace

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None in the Italian style; Alsace bottlings can age well

composition.process: Quick pressing keeps the greyish-pink skins from tinting the juice, which is what makes the Italian style so pale.

name: Retsina
description: An ancient Greek oddity infused with pine resin during fermentation, giving it an unmistakable forest-floor perfume. Divisive, historic, and stubbornly still here.
funFact: The style descends from antiquity, when amphorae were sealed with pine resin and the flavor seeped into the wine — Greeks came to like it that way.

serve.glass: White wine glass (or small taverna tumbler)
serve.how: Serve it very cold — chill tames the pine and turns divisive into delicious. Pour small amounts into a white wine glass or, more authentically, a little taverna tumbler, and drink it with food rather than alone. Give the resin a chance: after a bite of something garlicky or briny, the forest-floor perfume clicks into place like it has for two thousand years.

composition.summary: Savatiano and Roditis from Attica, infused with Aleppo pine resin during fermentation.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Savatiano mainly, with Roditis and occasionally Assyrtiko

components.label: Region
components.detail: Attica and central Greece, around Athens

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Aleppo pine resin added to the must during fermentation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; the resin is racked off with the lees and bottled young

composition.process: Pine resin steeped in the fermenting must — a survival of amphora sealing — becomes the flavor rather than the container.

name: Riesling
description: A high-acid chameleon that ranges from bone dry to nectar sweet while somehow always tasting like itself. With age it develops a curious and prized whiff of petrol.
funFact: Riesling's first documented mention dates to 1435, in the cellar inventory of a German count at Rüsselsheim.

serve.how: Check the label first — Trocken means dry, Kabinett and Spätlese lean sweeter — and chill accordingly, with sweeter styles taking a colder serve. Pour into a white wine glass, swirl, and smell for lime and peach; in older bottles, hunt for that prized, curious whiff of petrol. The electric acidity means even off-dry Rieslings finish clean, which makes them the great secret weapon against spicy food.

composition.summary: Riesling from Germany's steep slate river slopes, made bone dry to nectar sweet.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Riesling, documented in Germany since 1435

components.label: Region
components.detail: Mosel slate, Rheingau, Pfalz and Nahe; also Alsace and Clare Valley

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Fermentation halted where the grower wants it on the Prädikat scale

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Steel or large neutral Fuder casks; oak flavor is never welcome

composition.process: Stopping fermentation at a chosen point balances residual sugar against searing acidity, from trocken to lusciously sweet.

name: Sancerre
description: The most aristocratic form of Sauvignon Blanc, grown on flint and limestone hills overlooking the upper Loire. Smoky, precise, and perpetually in demand at wine bars.
funFact: Though famous for whites, the Sancerre appellation also covers reds and rosés made from Pinot Noir, a remnant of its pre-phylloxera past as red wine country.

serve.how: Serve it just cool, not cold — a few degrees warmer than everyday Sauvignon Blanc lets the smoky gunflint character surface over the grapefruit. Pour into a white wine glass, swirl, and take your time with the nose; the flint-and-chalk precision is what you paid for. Sip it alongside goat cheese and you'll taste one of the classic pairings in all of wine.
pair: crottin de Chavignol or any goat cheese

composition.summary: Sauvignon Blanc on the flint and limestone hills of the upper Loire.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Sauvignon Blanc for the whites; Pinot Noir for its reds and rosés

components.label: Region
components.detail: Sancerre, upper Loire, on terres blanches, caillottes and silex

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool steel fermentation; oak is used rarely and lightly

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Generally none; a few top cuvées see old barrels briefly

composition.process: Flint-rich silex soils and cold cellar fermentation give the smoky, gunflint edge that separates Sancerre from generic Sauvignon.

name: Sauvignon Blanc
description: A sharp, grassy creature that announces itself from across the room with a burst of gooseberry and cut grass. Thrives in the Loire, Marlborough, and refrigerators worldwide.
funFact: Its name derives from the French 'sauvage' (wild), and it is a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon via a chance crossing with Cabernet Franc.

serve.how: Serve it cold from the fridge, poured into a white wine glass, and drink it young — freshness is the entire point. No swirling ceremony required: the gooseberry and cut-grass aromatics announce themselves from across the room. Notice how the zippy acidity cuts through herbs, greens, and tangy cheeses that flatten other wines.

composition.summary: Sauvignon Blanc, wild-named grape of the Loire, Bordeaux and New Zealand's Marlborough.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Sauvignon Blanc; its name derives from 'sauvage', meaning wild

components.label: Region
components.detail: Loire Valley and Bordeaux in France; Marlborough in New Zealand

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool, protective fermentation preserves the thiols behind gooseberry and passionfruit

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Steel and young; white Bordeaux blends see barrel fermentation

composition.process: Fermenting cold and away from oxygen protects volatile thiol compounds — the source of that shout of cut grass.

name: Sémillon
description: A quiet, waxy grape that plays two extremes: the backbone of golden Sauternes in Bordeaux, and a lean, ageless dry white in Australia's Hunter Valley.
funFact: Hunter Valley Sémillon is picked early at low alcohol and tastes almost neutral in youth, then miraculously develops honeyed, toasty depth over decades in bottle.

serve.how: Serve dry Sémillon just lightly chilled in a white wine glass so the waxy, lanolin texture isn't numbed away. Swirl and look past the quiet lemon for beeswax and, in aged Hunter Valley bottles, an astonishing honeyed-toast depth that appears with a little air. If yours is a sweet Sauternes-style bottling instead, chill it harder and pour small glasses for after dinner.
pair: flaky white fish in butter sauce

composition.summary: Sémillon, botrytis vessel in Bordeaux and a lean, ageless dry white in Australia.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Sémillon; blended with Sauvignon Blanc in Bordeaux, solo in the Hunter

components.label: Region
components.detail: Sauternes and Graves in Bordeaux; the Hunter Valley, New South Wales

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Thin skins invite botrytis; the Hunter picks early at low alcohol

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Sauternes in barriques; Hunter Sémillon unoaked, then decades in bottle

composition.process: In the Hunter it is picked barely ripe and never oaked, so all its complexity develops later in bottle.

name: Soave
description: A gentle Venetian white built on the Garganega grape, all pear and almond softened by volcanic soils. Once dismissed as cheap, its hillside crus are quietly excellent.
funFact: In the 1970s Soave was the best-selling imported Italian wine in the United States, outselling even Chianti.

serve.how: Chill it down and pour into a white wine glass; single-vineyard Classico bottles deserve a slightly warmer serve and a moment to open. Swirl and find the gentle pear and melon, then wait for the signature bitter-almond note on the finish — that's the Garganega grape's calling card. It's a soft-spoken wine, so pair it with delicate food that won't shout over it.

composition.summary: Garganega grown on volcanic hills east of Verona in the Veneto.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Garganega mainly, with Trebbiano di Soave or Chardonnay permitted

components.label: Region
components.detail: Soave and Soave Classico, on volcanic basalt hills near Verona

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool steel fermentation; some producers rest it on fine lees

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Little to none; hillside crus and Riserva can take some wood

composition.process: Dark volcanic basalt on the Classico hills gives the salty, almond-skin bite that flatland Soave never manages.

name: Torrontés
description: Argentina's aromatic trickster: it smells sweet as a flower shop, then lands crisp and dry. Happiest in dizzyingly high desert vineyards.
funFact: Torrontés is a natural cross between Muscat of Alexandria and the Mission grape brought to the Americas by Spanish missionaries.

serve.how: Serve it cold in a white wine glass and enjoy the bait-and-switch: the nose promises a flower shop's worth of rose and muscat sweetness, then the palate lands crisp and dry. No decanting, no ceremony — just smell deeply before each sip to catch the perfume. It's built for aromatic, spiced food that matches its own volume.

composition.summary: Torrontés Riojano, an aromatic Argentine cross grown in high desert vineyards.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Torrontés Riojano; a Muscat of Alexandria × Criolla Chica cross

components.label: Region
components.detail: Cafayate in Salta, plus La Rioja and Mendoza, Argentina

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Pressed quickly off skins to keep bitterness out; fermented cold

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; steel and bottled young, with oak strictly avoided

composition.process: Fast pressing keeps its Muscat-derived terpenes aromatic without the phenolic bitterness those thick skins would otherwise contribute.

name: Txakoli
description: The Basque Country's electric, lightly fizzy white, low in alcohol and high in theatrics. Bartenders pour it from a great height to rouse its bubbles.
funFact: In San Sebastián's pintxo bars, Txakoli is traditionally poured from arm's length above the glass to aerate it and coax out its natural fizz.

serve.how: Chill it hard, then do it Basque-style: hold the bottle at arm's length above a flat tumbler and pour a long, thin stream to rouse the natural fizz — a few splashes on the counter are part of the ritual. Pour only a couple of inches at a time and drink it fast while it's cold and spritzy. Notice the green apple, lime, and saline crackle; at barely 11% alcohol it's made for grazing through snacks.

composition.summary: Hondarrabi Zuri from the Atlantic-lashed hills of the Basque Country.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Hondarrabi Zuri; the red Hondarrabi Beltza makes the rosé

components.label: Region
components.detail: Getariako, Bizkaiko and Arabako Txakolina, in Basque Spain

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Picked early at low ripeness; a light spritz retained at bottling

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; drunk within the year, ideally standing at a bar

composition.process: Early harvest in a cool, wet maritime climate keeps alcohol low and acidity high, with a faint prickle sealed in.

name: Vermentino
description: A sun-loving Mediterranean white with a pleasantly bitter, almond-skin farewell. It patrols the coasts of Sardinia, Liguria, and Corsica, where it moonlights as Rolle.
funFact: Vermentino di Gallura is the only DOCG, Italy's highest wine classification, on the entire island of Sardinia.

serve.how: Serve it fridge-cool in a white wine glass, ideally somewhere you can pretend there's a sea breeze. Swirl and taste for lime and green pear, then wait for the pleasantly bitter almond-skin farewell on the finish — that's the grape saying goodbye properly. It shines brightest with herb-flecked Mediterranean food and anything pulled from the sea.

composition.summary: Vermentino from Sardinia, Liguria and Corsica, where it also goes by Rolle.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Vermentino; Rolle in Provence, Pigato and Favorita in Italy

components.label: Region
components.detail: Sardinia's Gallura DOCG, plus Liguria, Tuscany, Corsica and Provence

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Cool steel fermentation; brief skin contact adds texture and grip

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually none; a few producers age briefly on lees

composition.process: A short spell on the skins draws out the phenolics behind that gently bitter, almond-skin finish.

name: Vinho Verde
description: Portugal's 'green wine' — green as in young, not in color. Low in alcohol, lightly spritzy, and best consumed within sight of a beach.
funFact: The gentle fizz was originally an accident of secondary fermentation in bottle; today many producers add a small dose of carbon dioxide on purpose.

serve.how: This is the rare wine you genuinely cannot serve too cold — bury it in ice and pour it into a white wine glass beaded with condensation. Drink it young, within a year of the vintage, and feel the gentle prickle of spritz over lime and green apple. At around 10% alcohol it's an afternoon wine; no swirling or ceremony, just keep it cold and keep it coming.

composition.summary: Loureiro, Alvarinho and Arinto from the wet green northwest of Portugal.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Loureiro, Alvarinho, Arinto, Trajadura and Avesso, usually blended

components.label: Region
components.detail: Minho, between the Douro and the Spanish border, Portugal

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Picked early for low alcohol; a dose of CO2 supplies the fizz

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; the whole style is built on youth and freshness

composition.process: The spritz began as accidental bottle refermentation and is now added deliberately, keeping a lean wine lively.

name: Viognier
description: A lush, apricot-scented rarity rescued from the brink of extinction. Full-bodied and heady, it walks the line between opulence and excess.
funFact: By the 1960s Viognier had dwindled to roughly a dozen acres in Condrieu before a global revival brought it back from near extinction.

serve.how: Serve it warmer than most whites — too much chill locks away the apricot-and-honeysuckle perfume that is Viognier's whole reason for being. Pour into a generous white wine glass, swirl slowly, and give it ten minutes; the nose blooms as it warms. Notice the lush, almost oily texture and keep pours modest, since its heady richness and higher alcohol walk the line between opulence and excess.

composition.summary: Viognier from Condrieu and Château-Grillet in the northern Rhône, rescued from near-extinction.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Viognier; reduced to roughly a dozen acres by the 1960s

components.label: Region
components.detail: Condrieu and Château-Grillet in the northern Rhône; now worldwide

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Picked very ripe for apricot terpenes; often barrel-fermented with lees stirring

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Neutral oak for a few months; malolactic softens the acidity

composition.process: It must be picked at full ripeness for its apricot perfume to appear, which is why the alcohol runs high.

name: Bacanora
description: Sonora's clandestine agave spirit, distilled from wild agave in mountain hideouts through nearly eight decades of prohibition. Smoky, mineral, and still carrying the swagger of the outlaw years.
funFact: Bacanora was outlawed in Sonora from 1915 until 1992, so generations of families kept the tradition alive with hidden stills in the sierra.

serve.how: Pour an ounce or two into a veladora and let it sit for a minute or two so the alcohol vapors lift off before you nose it. Sip neat in small draws, rolling the spirit across your tongue to catch the mineral edge and desert-herb notes beneath the light smoke. Skip ice entirely; dilution flattens the wild-agave character that makes bacanora worth hunting down.

composition.summary: Distilled from Sonoran agave, mostly the wild-harvested Agave angustifolia known locally as pacífico.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave angustifolia ('pacífico'), much of it still gathered wild

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, crushed, then run through small copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Almost always bottled unaged and clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–48% ABV

composition.process: Roasting the agave hearts in earth-and-stone pits is what lays down that mountain smoke.

name: Mezcal Añejo
description: Mezcal aged at least a year in oak, where smoke, caramel, and leather negotiate a rich truce. A rarity, since most mezcaleros prefer their spirit young and untamed.
funFact: Unlike tequila's single permitted species, mezcal may legally be produced from dozens of different agave varieties.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Serve neat in a snifter and give it one gentle swirl, then let it rest so the barrel notes open up. Nose it with your mouth slightly open to soften the smoke, and look for where the caramel and leather meet the char on the finish. If it runs hot, a single large cube tames the heat without erasing the oak.

composition.summary: Pit-roasted agave, pot-distilled, then left in oak for at least a year.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Espadín or other permitted agave species, pit-roasted

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper or clay pot stills, usually twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum one year in oak, per the mezcal standard

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–46% ABV

composition.process: A full year in wood is the negotiation that lets caramel and leather meet the smoke.

name: Mezcal de Pechuga
description: Ceremonial mezcal given a final distillation with seasonal fruits, spices, and a raw poultry breast suspended in the still. Brewed for weddings and saints' days, encountered by mortals almost never.
funFact: 'Pechuga' means 'breast' — traditionally a whole chicken or turkey breast hangs inside the still during the final pass, subtly rounding the spirit.

serve.how: Treat this like the ceremonial spirit it is: pour a small measure into a veladora, no ice, no mixing, and share it slowly with people you like. Take tiny sips and hunt for the stone fruit and holiday spice riding under the smoke, with that faint savory roundness from the pechuga itself on the finish. Let the glass sit between sips; it keeps evolving as it breathes.
pair: roast turkey or chicken with mole

composition.summary: Mezcal given a final still run with seasonal fruit, spices, and raw poultry breast.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Pit-roasted agave, plus fruit, nuts, spices and raw poultry

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: An extra pass with the breast suspended inside the still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged — bottled straight after the pechuga run

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 45–55% ABV

composition.process: That third distillation over hanging poultry strips harshness and rounds the spirit into ceremony.

name: Mezcal Joven
description: Unaged mezcal, where agave hearts roasted in earthen pits deliver their famous campfire smoke and wild fruit. Oaxaca's rawest, truest voice.
funFact: Mezcal's signature smokiness comes from roasting agave hearts for days in stone-lined pits dug into the earth.

serve.how: Pour a modest measure into a wide, shallow veladora and let it breathe for a minute before nosing. Kiss it rather than gulp it: small sips held on the palate reveal tropical fruit and wet-stone minerality behind the campfire smoke. Traditional accompaniments are orange slices dusted with sal de gusano, not lime and shot glasses.
pair: orange slices with sal de gusano

composition.summary: Unaged mezcal from agave hearts roasted in earthen pits and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave hearts, most often cultivated espadín

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small copper or clay pot stills, typically twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None — bottled clear and straight off the still

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–52% ABV

composition.process: Days of roasting in stone-lined earth pits is the single step that makes mezcal smoky.

name: Mezcal Reposado
description: Mezcal rested briefly in wood, letting vanilla and honey settle over the smoke like dusk over a cookfire. A gentler on-ramp to the smoky arts.
funFact: Around nine in every ten bottles of mezcal are made from a single cultivated agave, espadín, prized for its relatively quick maturation.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Sip it neat from a veladora to catch the honey and vanilla the barrel has draped over the smoke, taking your time between small pours. This is the friendliest on-ramp to mezcal, so if the smoke still reads strong, a single large cube softens it into something almost dessert-like. Notice how the roasted agave core stays intact under the oak polish.

composition.summary: Pit-roasted agave mezcal rested a few months in wood before bottling.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Pit-roasted agave, usually espadín

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper or clay pot stills, generally twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak from two months up to a year

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–48% ABV

composition.process: A short rest in wood lays vanilla and honey over the smoke without burying it.

name: Mezcal Tobalá
description: Mezcal from the small, wild tobalá agave that hides in high mountain canyons and yields only a fraction of what farmed espadín gives. Often crowned 'the king of mezcals.'
funFact: Tobalá agave produces no clones or offshoots — it reproduces only by seed in the wild, which is a big reason it stays scarce and expensive.

serve.how: Pour sparingly, this is scarce juice, and let the glass sit for several minutes; tobala's floral perfume needs air to bloom. Sip in small, slow draws and chase the wild fruit and wet-stone notes that float above the gentle smoke. No ice, no citrus, no mixing: at this rarity you are tasting a plant that took a decade to grow in a mountain canyon.

composition.summary: Mezcal from wild tobalá agave, a small canyon-dwelling species that yields very little.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wild Agave potatorum, harvested from high mountain canyons

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, then twice through small copper or clay stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged, so the wild agave stays the loudest voice

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 45–50% ABV

composition.process: It takes several times more tobalá hearts than espadín to fill a bottle.

name: Raicilla
description: West Jalisco's backwoods agave spirit, long distilled off the books in the sierra and along the coast — funky, fruity, and less smoky than its Oaxacan cousins. Mezcal's mischievous mountain kin.
funFact: Raicilla — 'little root' — reputedly got its name as a colonial-era tax dodge, and it finally received its own denomination of origin in 2019.

serve.how: Serve neat at room temperature in a veladora and nose it first: raicilla leads with ripe fruit and wild funk rather than smoke, so expect something closer to a natural wine's aromatics. Sip slowly and let it coat the palate, watching for the green agave brightness underneath the fermented-fruit character. Keep it away from ice and mixers until you have met it on its own terms.
pair: tropical fruit with chile and lime

composition.summary: Western Jalisco agave spirit from mountain and coastal species, cooked without heavy smoke.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Local Jalisco agaves such as maximiliana and inaequidens

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or filipino-style stills, often clay or wood-fired

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged, bottled clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–48% ABV

composition.process: Many producers cook the agave in above-ground ovens, which is why it reads fruity, not smoky.

name: Sotol
description: The spirit of the Chihuahuan Desert, distilled from the wild desert spoon plant into something grassy, mineral, and quietly feral. Tastes like the high desert after rain.
funFact: Despite being shelved with agave spirits, sotol is not made from agave at all — the desert spoon is a different plant that can take around 15 years to mature.

serve.how: Pour a small measure neat and give it a minute of air, then nose gently: sotol smells like the high desert after rain, all grass, pine, and mineral. Sip slowly and let it sit on the mid-palate, where the earthy, vegetal side unfolds; it is drier and greener than mezcal, so do not go looking for sweetness. Room temperature keeps those delicate herbal notes alive.

composition.summary: Distilled from the wild desert spoon plant, not agave at all.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wild Dasylirion — desert spoon — harvested across the Chihuahuan Desert

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Roasted, crushed, then run through small pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Most is unaged; some producers rest it briefly in oak

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–48% ABV

composition.process: The plants are gathered wild from desert hillsides, so the spirit changes with the terrain.

name: Tequila Añejo
description: Tequila aged one to three years, trading youthful bite for caramel, chocolate, and dried fruit. Proof that agave can play in whiskey's league.
funFact: By law, añejo must age in oak barrels no larger than 600 liters, which keeps the wood's influence concentrated.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Treat anejo like a fine whiskey: pour into a snifter, swirl once, and let it rest a few minutes before nosing for caramel, chocolate, and cooked agave. Sip neat and slow, noting how the oak frames the agave rather than burying it. A single large cube is fine on a warm night, but skip crushed ice and mixers, this earned its barrel time.

composition.summary: Blue Weber agave tequila aged one to three years in oak barrels.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Blue Weber agave, steam-cooked in ovens or autoclaves

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled at least twice, usually in copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: One to three years in oak casks no larger than 600 litres

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–40% ABV

composition.process: Small barrels concentrate wood contact, pushing agave toward caramel and chocolate.

name: Tequila Blanco
description: Tequila in its purest form, bottled fresh from the still so the roasted blue agave speaks without oak interrupting. Peppery, vegetal, and vividly alive.
funFact: A blue Weber agave typically grows for six to eight years before a jimador harvests its heart, called the piña for its resemblance to a pineapple.

serve.how: Pour a couple of ounces into a caballito and sip, do not shoot; blanco is the purest expression of roasted blue agave and rewards patience. Take small sips and look for white pepper, citrus, and green herbs riding over the sweet agave core. A slight chill crisps it up in summer, but avoid heavy icing, which mutes the vegetal brightness.

composition.summary: Unaged tequila distilled purely from cooked blue Weber agave.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Blue Weber agave piñas, steam-cooked until sweet

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Twice through copper pot or column stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None, or a brief rest in steel — bottled clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–46% ABV

composition.process: Skipping the barrel entirely leaves the cooked agave with nothing to hide behind.

name: Tequila Cristalino
description: Aged tequila filtered through charcoal until it runs crystal clear, keeping barrel softness while shedding barrel color. Alchemy for drinkers who want their añejo invisible.
funFact: The cristalino craze is usually traced to Don Julio 70, launched in 2011 as the first widely marketed clear añejo.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Serve in a rocks glass either neat or over one large, slow-melting cube; cristalino is built for smooth, easy sipping. Notice the trick of it: the vanilla and soft caramel of an aged tequila with none of the color, and a finish that snaps clean like a blanco. It also makes a luxurious base for an ultra-clear Margarita or Paloma if you tire of sipping.

composition.summary: Aged tequila filtered through charcoal until the barrel colour is stripped out.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Blue Weber agave, cooked and fermented as usual

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled twice, then aged before the filtration step

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Reposado, añejo or extra añejo stock, later stripped clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 35–40% ABV

composition.process: Activated-charcoal filtration pulls the colour out while leaving much of the barrel sweetness behind.

name: Tequila Extra Añejo
description: Ultra-aged tequila that slumbers in oak for at least three years, emerging dark, plush, and cognac-like. The category tequila invented once it started wearing suits.
funFact: Extra añejo is the newest official tequila classification, created only in 2006 as producers pushed into luxury territory.

serve.how: Pour a small measure into a snifter, cup the bowl in your palm to warm it slightly, and give it several minutes to open. Sip in tiny draws the way you would a cognac, tracking the dark caramel, dried fruit, and polished oak through a long finish. No ice and no mixing; at three-plus years in barrel, dilution only steals what you paid for.

composition.summary: Blue Weber agave tequila aged a minimum of three years in oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Blue Weber agave, steam-cooked and fermented

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: At least two passes, typically copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in oak barrels up to 600 litres

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually bottled at 40% ABV

composition.process: Years of oak push agave into cognac territory — dark, plush, and slow.

name: Tequila Joven
description: The 'young' or gold style, usually a blanco softened with a splash of aged tequila or a touch of color and sweetness. The tequila of a million spring-break stories.
funFact: Most inexpensive 'gold' tequila gets its color from added caramel coloring rather than from time spent in a barrel.

serve.how: Joven is the party style, so chill it down and serve in caballitos, ideally with sangrita or citrus on the side rather than the salt-and-lime slam. If sipping, look for the caramel sweetness layered over young agave and mild pepper. It is also happiest in a Margarita or tequila sunrise, where its softened edges are a feature, not a flaw.

composition.summary: Blue Weber agave tequila, usually blanco blended with aged tequila or colouring.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Blue Weber agave, cooked and fermented like any tequila

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Standard double distillation in pot or column stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Mostly unaged — colour often comes from additives, not barrels

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–40% ABV

composition.process: Blending or colouring a blanco gives the look of barrel time without the barrel.

name: Tequila Reposado
description: Tequila 'rested' in oak for two months to a year, just long enough to drape vanilla and soft spice over the agave without smothering it. The diplomatic middle ground.
funFact: Reposado literally means 'rested,' and much of the resting happens in used American bourbon barrels shipped south across the border.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour into a rocks glass neat or over a single large cube and give it a short rest; reposado's vanilla and baking spice bloom with a little air. Sip and notice the balance point, enough oak to round the edges, enough agave to remember where it came from. It is also the sweet spot for an elevated Margarita or Old Fashioned riff.

composition.summary: Blue Weber agave tequila rested in oak from two months to a year.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Blue Weber agave, steam-cooked and fermented

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Twice distilled in copper pot or column stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Two to twelve months, frequently in used American whiskey barrels

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–40% ABV

composition.process: Just enough time in wood to drape vanilla over the agave without smothering it.

name: Aperol
description: Campari's sunnier, gentler sibling, glowing neon orange and only lightly bitter. In spritz form it has colonized patios across the entire planet.
funFact: Aperol was created in 1919 by brothers Luigi and Silvio Barbieri of Padua and carries roughly half the alcohol of its rival Campari.

serve.temp: well chilled (38-45°F), served over plenty of ice
serve.how: Keep the bottle in the fridge and build the classic Spritz in a big wine glass: fill with ice, pour 3 parts chilled prosecco, 2 parts Aperol, 1 part soda, and garnish with an orange slice. Stir once, gently, so the Aperol does not sink and sulk at the bottom. Sip it slowly outdoors before dinner; the gentle rhubarb-orange bitterness is designed to wake up your appetite, not test it.

composition.summary: A low-proof Italian bitter aperitif built on neutral spirit and botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit, water and sugar carrying an orange-led infusion

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Not distilled as such — botanicals are infused, then blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; bottled bright and fresh

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 11% ABV, roughly half its scarlet rival

composition.process: Bitter and sweet orange, rhubarb and gentian are infused and sweetened into that neon glow.

name: Campari
description: The scarlet gatekeeper of the aperitivo hour, bitter as a grudge and bright as a sunset. It tests new trainers with grapefruit-pith bitterness before rewarding them for life.
funFact: Campari's famous red color came from carmine dye made from cochineal insects until the company switched to artificial coloring in 2006.

serve.how: Serve over a large cube with a fat orange peel, or lengthen with soda in a highball for the classic Campari e soda. Sip slowly and let your palate acclimate: the first taste is a grapefruit-pith wallop, but by the third sip the herbs and cherry underneath start rewarding you. Keep it as a pre-dinner ritual, its bitterness is engineered to sharpen the appetite.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit infused with bitter herbs and fruit peel, sweetened and bottled red.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit, water and sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: An infusion, not a distillate — herbs and peels steep in spirit

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Varies by market, roughly 20.5–28.5% ABV

composition.process: A secret herb-and-peel infusion delivers that grapefruit-pith bitterness the whole aperitivo hour rests on.

name: Cynar
description: An amaro that proudly wears an artichoke on its label, yet tastes of caramelized herbs rather than vegetables. A gentle, vegetal riddle beloved in low-proof cocktails.
funFact: Launched in 1952, Cynar takes its name from Cynara scolymus, the artichoke, one of thirteen herbs and plants in its recipe.

serve.how: Pour over a big cube with an orange twist, or top with soda water and a pinch of salt for the Italian classic. Sip slowly and notice the riddle: cola and caramelized-herb sweetness up front, a gentle vegetal bitterness on the back, and no actual artichoke flavor anywhere. Its low proof makes it a perfect unhurried afternoon or after-dinner drink.

composition.summary: An Italian bitter liqueur infused with thirteen herbs and plants, artichoke included.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit infused with artichoke and twelve other botanicals

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Made by maceration and blending rather than redistillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: Artichoke leaf does the bittering work, but caramel sweetness keeps it from tasting like a vegetable.

name: Fernet-Branca
description: A menthol-black Italian amaro of legendary intensity, brewed from 27 secret herbs. Feared by novices, worshipped by bartenders, and consumed by Argentina in heroic quantities.
funFact: Argentina drinks well over 70% of all Fernet-Branca produced, mostly mixed with cola in the beloved fernet con coca.

serve.glass: Shot glass or small chilled rocks glass
serve.how: Pour a small measure neat as a digestif after a heavy meal; the menthol-and-bitter-herb blast is the point, so take it in confident sips rather than nervous ones. A light chill softens the eucalyptus edge for newcomers, but true believers drink it room temperature. For the Argentine experience, pour an ounce or two over ice and top generously with cola for a fernet con coca.

composition.summary: A ferociously bitter Milanese amaro built from twenty-seven herbs and spices.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grape spirit infused with twenty-seven herbs, roots and spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Botanicals are macerated and infused, then blended to recipe

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak casks before bottling

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 39% ABV

composition.process: Myrrh, saffron and menthol-heavy botanicals are steeped until the result tastes like medicine that won.

name: American Single Malt
description: One hundred percent malted barley from a single American distillery — Scotland's blueprint rebuilt with New World swagger. The newest official branch of the whiskey family tree.
funFact: American single malt only became an officially recognized U.S. whiskey category when the TTB finalized its rule in December 2024.

serve.how: Pour a standard dram into a Glencairn, swirl gently, and nose in short sniffs with your mouth slightly open to catch malt, chocolate, and orchard fruit. Sip neat first, then add a few drops of water to unlock the toasted-oak depths; many American single malts run above 43% and open beautifully. Compare it mentally to Scotch, the malt DNA is the same but the New World oak speaks louder.

composition.summary: One hundred percent malted barley, distilled and matured at a single American distillery.

components.label: Base
components.detail: All malted barley, no other grain permitted

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled at one US distillery, pot stills most common

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak casks up to 700 litres; new charred oak not required

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 43–50% ABV

composition.process: Scotland's all-malt blueprint, but with American oak, climate and no regional rulebook.

name: Bottled-in-Bond Bourbon
description: Whiskey with a government-stamped pedigree: one distillery, one distilling season, at least four years in a bonded warehouse, and exactly 100 proof. No fudging allowed.
funFact: The Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897 was one of America's earliest consumer-protection laws, arriving nine years before the Pure Food and Drug Act.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour neat into a Glencairn and let the 100-proof pour sit a couple of minutes before nosing for toffee, leather, and baking spice. Sip slowly; bonded bourbon is built to a standard, not a price, so the extra proof carries flavor rather than just heat. A few drops of water or one large cube will unwrap the oak if the finish runs hot.

composition.summary: Bourbon from one distillery and one season, aged four years, bottled at 100 proof.

components.label: Base
components.detail: At least 51% corn, like any bourbon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: One distillery, one distilling season, no blending across either

components.label: Aging
components.detail: At least four years in a federally bonded warehouse

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Exactly 50% ABV — 100 proof, no negotiation

composition.process: The 1897 Bond Act ties provenance, age and proof to a government stamp.

name: Bourbon
description: America's signature whiskey, born of a corn-heavy mash and new charred oak. Sweet, sturdy, and sociable — it appears anywhere Americans gather to argue about whiskey.
funFact: In 1964 the U.S. Congress declared bourbon a distinctive product of the United States, though it can legally be made in any state, not just Kentucky.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour two fingers into a rocks glass and try it neat first, nosing for caramel, vanilla, and charred oak before the first sip. Let each sip rest on the tongue a beat so the corn sweetness spreads before the oak spice arrives. One large cube slowly opens it up on a warm evening, and if you would rather go long, bourbon and ginger ale is a forgiving classic.

composition.summary: American whiskey from a mash of at least 51% corn, aged in new charred oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Minimum 51% corn, rounded out with rye, wheat or malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still and doubler, distilled to no more than 160 proof

components.label: Aging
components.detail: New charred oak containers; 'straight' bourbon needs two years

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–50% ABV

composition.process: Fresh charred oak, used exactly once, is what gives bourbon its caramel and vanilla.

name: Cask Strength Bourbon
description: Bourbon bottled straight from the barrel with no dilution — whiskey with the volume knob snapped off. Approach with water, patience, or bravado.
funFact: Bourbon may legally enter the barrel at no more than 125 proof, but years of evaporation in hot rickhouses can push some barrel-proof releases above 70% ABV.

serve.temp: room temp, with water on standby
serve.how: Pour a smaller-than-usual measure into a Glencairn and approach in stages: nose gently from a distance first, since 60%-plus alcohol will singe an eager nostril. Take a tiny first sip to calibrate, then add water a few drops at a time, tasting between additions until the burnt sugar and dark cherry bloom out of the heat. Finding each barrel's ideal dilution point is the whole sport.
